skills.title: Safety licence
skills.objective: Recognize workshop hazards, prepare safely, and report problems promptly.

checkpoints.title: Know the room
checkpoints.practice: Take an instructor-led tour. Locate the exits, fire extinguisher, first aid kit, emergency stops, and cleanup supplies. Repeat the route independently and explain when to alert an instructor.
checkpoints.criteria: Locate the five safety and cleanup points without prompts.

checkpoints.title: Dress for it
checkpoints.practice: Prepare for each session with closed shoes, secured hair, fitted clothing, and the required eye protection. Ask an instructor to record your readiness across three consecutive sessions.
checkpoints.criteria: Arrive correctly prepared for three consecutive sessions.

checkpoints.title: The hot and sharp list
checkpoints.practice: Discuss the hazards of soldering equipment, hot printer components, cutting tools, solvents, and batteries. For each example, name a specific hazard, a precaution, and the point at which you would stop and ask for help.
checkpoints.criteria: Explain specific hazards and precautions for the equipment discussed.

checkpoints.title: Speak up
checkpoints.practice: Work through instructor-provided incident scenarios. Practise stopping work, moving clear when safe, and reporting the problem promptly. Do not attempt an unfamiliar repair or hide a mistake.
checkpoints.criteria: Choose immediate staff reporting in the scenario discussion.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: Licence. Access remains subject to workshop safety rules.
skills.unlocks: Access to appropriate workshop benches and all later Academy pathways.

skills.title: Workspace discipline
skills.objective: Set up, clean, store unfinished work, and manage shared equipment responsibly.

checkpoints.title: Find it without asking
checkpoints.practice:
You need to know where things live.

Pick up a job. Get everything you need for it without asking a staff member where anything is.
checkpoints.criteria: Independently prepare a familiar task in under five minutes.

checkpoints.title: Put it away properly
checkpoints.practice:
The end of a session is part of the session.

1. Tools back where they came from
2. Offcuts and scrap in the right bin, and we do sort scrap here
3. Bench wiped
4. Your work in your named bin, labelled so the next person knows not to touch it
5. Chair in
checkpoints.criteria: Leave the workspace ready for another person to use immediately.

checkpoints.title: Leave a job properly
checkpoints.practice:
Unfinished work is normal. Losing track of unfinished work is not.

When you stop mid project:

1. Loose parts in a bag or tub, not loose in the bin
2. A note in the bin saying where you got to and what is next
3. Anything drying or curing goes on the shelf, labelled with your name and the date
checkpoints.criteria: Store parts and notes so work can resume a week later.

checkpoints.title: Shared kit
checkpoints.practice:
Some things belong to everybody. The good files, the vise, the paint, the cutting mat.

1. Ask before you take something off somebody else's bench
2. Put shared kit back clean, not just back
3. Explain to your instructor when something is running out, before it runs out
4. Explain to your instructor when something is broken, even if it was not you
checkpoints.criteria: Proactively report depleted or damaged shared supplies.

skills.title: The maker's notebook
skills.objective: Record settings, decisions, failures, and next steps in a useful workshop notebook.

checkpoints.title: Set it up
checkpoints.practice:
Five minutes, once.

1. Your name on the front, and the date you started it.
2. Leave the first two pages empty. That becomes your contents list when you have something worth finding.
3. Rule a margin down the left of a page. Numbers go in the margin, words go beside them.
4. That margin is the whole trick. It means you can find a number later without reading a paragraph.
checkpoints.criteria: Keep a named notebook in the project bin.

checkpoints.title: One session, written down
checkpoints.practice:
Work a normal session and write it as you go.

By the end we want to see, on the page:

1. The date.
2. What you were making.
3. At least three real numbers.
4. One thing that did not work.
5. One line starting with next time.
checkpoints.criteria: Document a session so another person can reconstruct its work and cost.

checkpoints.title: Use it to win
checkpoints.practice:
Notes are worth nothing until they save you once.

Come back to a job you did before, look up your own numbers, and use them instead of guessing.

This will happen naturally within a few weeks. When it does, mark the page.
checkpoints.criteria: Use a recorded setting to achieve a correct setup immediately.

checkpoints.title: Pass it on
checkpoints.practice:
Somebody else has a problem you have already had.

Find it in your book and read it to them. Do not hand them the book and do not do the job for them.
checkpoints.criteria: Help another person succeed using your notes.

skills.title: Sort the scrap
skills.objective: Identify, sort, weigh, record, and reuse workshop scrap.

checkpoints.title: Name it by hand
checkpoints.practice:
We hand you six pieces off the bench with no labels.

You get to bend them, snap them and look at them. You do not get to smell the spool it came from, because there is no spool.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify at least five of six samples and explain the evidence.

checkpoints.title: Sort a real bin
checkpoints.practice:
Take a full scrap bin from a printer and empty it onto the sorting mat.

1. Three tubs out, labelled.
2. Sort the whole bin. All of it, not the easy half.
3. Anything you cannot identify goes to waste, and you say so out loud rather than quietly hoping.
4. Gloves for this one and wash your hands after. Scrap has been on a lot of surfaces.
checkpoints.criteria: Correctly sort a real batch, keeping reusable material clean.

checkpoints.title: Weigh it and log it
checkpoints.practice:
The scale lives at the scrap station and the log lives beside it.

1. Weigh each tub.
2. Write the date, the weights and your name in the log.
3. Look at last month's numbers and say whether this week is normal, high or low.
4. This workshop throws away more plastic than most people expect. Knowing the number is the first step to it going down.
checkpoints.criteria: Log three weights and identify the largest printer waste source.

checkpoints.title: Make something out of it
checkpoints.practice:
The point of the shelf.

Take a piece off the usable tub and turn it into something you actually needed. A spacer, a shim, a handle, a jig block, a test coupon.

It does not have to be pretty. It has to be a thing you would otherwise have printed.
checkpoints.criteria: Make a useful object from scrap and quantify avoided printing time.

skills.title: Ask a good question
skills.objective: Investigate problems, explain expectations, show evidence, and recognize urgent issues.

checkpoints.title: Try three things
checkpoints.practice:
Before you ask a person, try three things and remember what they were.

Good three things:

1. Read the step again
2. Read the WHEN IT GOES WRONG list
3. Check the glossary for the word you are not sure about
4. Undo the last thing you did and watch what changes
checkpoints.criteria: Describe three reasonable attempts made before asking for help.

checkpoints.title: Say what you expected
checkpoints.practice:
A good question has three parts and takes about ten seconds.

1. What you were trying to do
2. What you expected to happen
3. What actually happened
4. "It is not working" is none of those.
5. "I set supports to tree and expected them under the arm, but the preview has none there" is all three, and we can answer it without walking over.
checkpoints.criteria: Ask three consecutive questions with the required context.

checkpoints.title: Show, do not tell
checkpoints.practice:
Bring the thing.

Bring the part, the screen, the board, the failed print. Do not describe it from memory and do not clear it away before you come and get us.

The failed print is the evidence. If you scrape it off the plate before we see it, we are both guessing.
checkpoints.criteria: Present observable evidence when describing a problem.

checkpoints.title: Know when not to wait
checkpoints.practice:
Some things you do not try three things first. You come and get us immediately.

1. Anything hot, sharp, smoking or sparking
2. A machine making a new noise
3. Something is broken
4. Somebody is hurt
5. You are about to do something you are not sure is safe
6. Waiting your turn is for questions. It is not for any of these.
checkpoints.criteria: Distinguish routine questions from issues requiring immediate intervention.

skills.title: Working in twos
skills.objective: Divide a shared build, work independently, hand over clearly, and credit contributions.

checkpoints.title: Split it on paper
checkpoints.practice:
Pick a real job that is genuinely too big for one person in the time you have.

1. Write the whole job as a list of steps.
2. Put a name against every step. Every one.
3. Mark the steps that cannot start until another step is done.
4. Agree who is doing the least interesting job on the list, and write that name down first.
checkpoints.criteria: Assign one owner to every task in a written plan.

checkpoints.title: Work it without narrating
checkpoints.practice:
Now do a session on it.

The thing we are watching for is silence that is comfortable. Two people working on their own halves, checking in occasionally, not managing each other.
checkpoints.criteria: Both partners spend most of the session doing useful work.

checkpoints.title: The handover
checkpoints.practice:
The session ends and the job is not finished. This is normal and it is the point.

One of you writes the handover note for the bin:

1. Where the job got to.
2. What is next, and whose list it is on.
3. Anything that will bite the next person. A joint that is still curing, a setting that got changed, a part that is not glued yet even though it looks glued.
checkpoints.criteria: Write a handover that lets the partner continue independently.

checkpoints.title: Finish it and say who did what
checkpoints.practice:
Finish the job.

Then, in front of us, each of you names one thing the other person did better than you would have.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete the build and accurately explain each person's contribution.

skills.title: Closing crew
skills.objective: Follow closing checks, inspect zones, report faults, and close the workshop.

checkpoints.title: Walk it with us
checkpoints.practice:
Close alongside a staff member, with the card, twice.

Ask what each line is actually for. Every one of them exists because of something that happened here.
checkpoints.criteria: Attend two closings and explain at least four checklist items.

checkpoints.title: Close a zone on your own
checkpoints.practice:
You take one zone. The printers, or the electronics bench, or the finishing bench.

Work the card for your zone alone, then hand it to us.
checkpoints.criteria: Close an assigned zone with no omissions found in inspection.

checkpoints.title: Report what you found
checkpoints.practice:
Closing is the workshop's daily inspection, and the report is the valuable part.

At the end, explain to your instructor:

1. Anything running low.
2. Any machine that is not right, even slightly.
3. Anything left out that has no name on it.
4. Never nothing. There is always something. A closing where nothing is reported is a closing where nobody looked.
checkpoints.criteria: Report a real issue that staff had not already noticed.

checkpoints.title: Close the whole floor
checkpoints.practice:
The full card, every zone, with a staff member present but not helping.

The last half of the card, the power and the doors, is done together. That does not change with this badge or any other.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete a correct, honestly recorded full closing, signed by staff.

skills.title: Plan a project
skills.objective: Define a project, test its main risk, update the plan, and finish against agreed criteria.

checkpoints.title: Write the card
checkpoints.practice:
Fill all five sections for a real project you actually want to make.

Size it honestly. Two sessions is a good first project. Six is a good second one. Ten is a thing people announce and never finish, and we have a wall of those in our heads.
checkpoints.criteria: Present a complete project card with a drawing and measurable finish criteria.

checkpoints.title: Find the risk and do it first
checkpoints.practice:
Circle the step that could sink it.

Then move it to the front, and do it in your first working session. Not the whole thing. The smallest version of it that proves it works.

A test print of the joint. A breadboard of the circuit. One scene of the game. One coat on a scrap piece.
checkpoints.criteria: Test the highest-risk element before investing in the remaining build.

checkpoints.title: Work the plan and keep it honest
checkpoints.practice:
Run at least three sessions on it.

At the end of each one, update the card in a different colour. What actually took how long. What moved. What you cut.

Cut something. Everybody cuts something. The people who do not cut anything do not finish.
checkpoints.criteria: Keep the project card aligned with actual scope and decisions.

checkpoints.title: Finish it and close it out
checkpoints.practice:
Hit the done line you wrote at the start.

Then write the last three lines in your notebook:

1. What took much longer than you thought.
2. What you would do differently.
3. What the next project is.
checkpoints.criteria: Deliver the agreed result and clear the project shelf.

skills.title: Peer coaching
skills.objective: Coach through questions and documentation while leaving the learner in control.

checkpoints.title: Ask before you tell
checkpoints.practice:
Start with a question, not an answer.

Good openers:

1. What are you trying to do
2. What did you expect
3. What have you tried
4. Show me
5. Nine times out of ten they work it out while they are answering you. That is the best possible outcome and you did it by saying almost nothing.
checkpoints.criteria: Help someone progress without supplying the answer.

checkpoints.title: Send them to the document
checkpoints.practice:
You are not the curriculum. The badge document is.

When they ask, find the step with them and read it together. Point at the line.

This matters because you will not always be here, and because a kid who learns to read the doc stops needing either of us.
checkpoints.criteria: Quickly locate relevant steps in badges you already hold.

checkpoints.title: Hands off
checkpoints.practice:
The hard one.

1. You may point
2. You may demonstrate on your own piece or on scrap
3. You may not touch their work
4. You may not hold it for them unless they ask and it is a safety thing
5. If they are about to do something unsafe, stop them. That is not coaching, that is the workshop.
checkpoints.criteria: Let the learner complete the work without taking over.

checkpoints.title: Coach somebody through a pass
checkpoints.practice:
The real one.

Take somebody through a checkpoint on a badge you already hold. They get assessed by us. They pass.

You do not get this one if they fail, and that is fair, because coaching somebody to almost ready is not coaching.
checkpoints.criteria: Coach someone whose completed work earns staff sign-off.

skills.title: Hand tool licence
skills.objective: Identify hand tools, secure work, file accurately, and restore the tool wall.

checkpoints.title: Name the wall
checkpoints.practice:
Walk the wall with us and name what is on it.

You need these by name, not by pointing:

1. Flat, half round and round files, and needle files.
2. Craft knife, snips, side cutters, and the razor saw.
3. Flat and cross head drivers, and the hex keys.
4. Long nose, flat nose and slip joint pliers.
5. The vise, the bench hook, and the mitre box.
6. The clamps, and where the soft jaws live.
checkpoints.criteria: Name eight selected tools and explain their appropriate uses.

checkpoints.title: Hold the work
checkpoints.practice:
Almost every hand tool injury in a workshop like this comes from holding the work in your hand.

1. Vise for anything you are sawing, filing or drilling.
2. Soft jaws for printed parts and anything painted. Steel jaws mark plastic in one squeeze.
3. Bench hook for anything you are cutting with the razor saw.
4. Tighten until it holds, not until it creaks. Printed parts crush.
checkpoints.criteria: Secure three jobs correctly without reminders.

checkpoints.title: File a flat
checkpoints.practice:
The first real hand skill, and the one that teaches your hands what a tool wants.

Take a scrap printed block and file one face flat and square.

1. Work in the vise, the face just above the jaws.
2. Push strokes only. A file cuts on the push. Dragging it back blunts it and does nothing.
3. Long strokes, whole face, using the whole file, not the middle six inches of it.
4. Check with a square, not with your eye, every dozen strokes.
5. Brush the file out. A loaded file scratches instead of cutting.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a face that checks flat and square along its length.

checkpoints.title: Put it back
checkpoints.practice:
The half of the licence people forget about.

1. Every tool wiped and back on its outline.
2. Blades retracted or capped.
3. Vise closed with a small gap and the handle turned down, not sticking out.
4. Filings and dust brushed off the bench into the bin, not onto the floor.
5. Anything damaged reported before you leave.
checkpoints.criteria: Return tools so the complete wall can be checked visually.

skills.title: Measure and mark
skills.objective: Measure with rulers and calipers, mark accurately, and inspect another person's part.

checkpoints.title: Read it right
checkpoints.practice:
We hand you five things and you explain to your instructor how big they are.

Rule for the big ones, calipers for the small ones, and you choose which is which.
checkpoints.criteria: Measure five objects within 0.5 mm of the reference values.

checkpoints.title: The caliper habits
checkpoints.practice:
Calipers are easy to use and easy to use badly.

1. Zero them closed, every single time, before the measurement.
2. Square onto the feature. At an angle you will read big.
3. Firm, not crushing. Printed plastic squeezes and you will read small.
4. Three measurements in three places on anything round, because printed holes are not round.
checkpoints.criteria: Repeat measurements reliably using external, internal, and depth features.

checkpoints.title: Mark it and cut to it
checkpoints.practice:
Take a piece of scrap and cut a piece exactly 60mm long off it.

1. Measure and mark a fine line.
2. Cross the waste side.
3. Measure your mark before you cut.
4. Cut on the waste side of the line, leaving the line.
5. Measure the result.
checkpoints.criteria: Cut a 60 mm piece within 0.5 mm and explain the cut position.

checkpoints.title: Check somebody else's work
checkpoints.practice:
The skill that makes you useful.

Take a part somebody else has made, or a printed part off the shelf, and measure it against what it is supposed to be.

Report the difference as a number and a direction. Not wrong. 0.4mm oversize on the boss.
checkpoints.criteria: Find and numerically report an actual dimensional discrepancy.

skills.title: Cut it straight
skills.objective: Use knives, flush cutters, and saws to produce clean cuts and change blades safely.

checkpoints.title: Score and snap
checkpoints.practice:
On card or thin sheet, with a steel rule and a knife.

1. Rule held down hard, fingers well back from the edge.
2. Blade against the rule, light first pass.
3. Three or four more passes, same line, same pressure.
4. Snap or cut through on the last pass.
checkpoints.criteria: Make a clean scored edge while keeping fingers clear.

checkpoints.title: Flush cut
checkpoints.practice:
Take a printed part with supports or a sprue still on it.

1. Snips flat side against the part.
2. Cut proud first, leaving a little.
3. Then a second cut flush.
4. Then a file or a knife to clean it, not more snipping.
5. Cutting flush in one go is how you take a divot out of the part.
checkpoints.criteria: Remove a nub flush without gouging or stressing the surface.

checkpoints.title: Saw something square
checkpoints.practice:
Razor saw, mitre box, bench hook.

1. Mark your line all the way round the part.
2. Start the cut with the saw pulled backwards a few times to make a groove.
3. Long, light strokes. Let the saw's weight do it.
4. Check the line on the far side before you are halfway through.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a square saw cut without damaging the exit side.

checkpoints.title: Change a blade
checkpoints.practice:
Nobody uses a blade you cannot change safely.

1. Blade goes in the sharps tin, never the bin.
2. New blade handled by its back edge only.
3. Handle locked and checked before it goes near the work.
4. Cap on, tool back in the drawer.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate a safe blade change and correct sharps disposal.

skills.title: Screws and threads
skills.objective: Identify screws, select drivers, fasten into plastic, and specify suitable hardware.

checkpoints.title: Sort and name
checkpoints.practice:
We tip out a tray of mixed fasteners.

Sort them by type and size and put them where they belong in the drawers.

You need to be able to say M3 or M2.5 by eye and confirm it with the gauge or the calipers.
checkpoints.criteria: Sort screws and correctly identify five selected sizes and lengths.

checkpoints.title: Driver fit
checkpoints.practice:
Lay out the drivers and the bits.

For each of five screws, pick the correct driver and show your instructor why the next size down is wrong.

Cross head sizes are PH0, PH1, PH2 and they are not interchangeable no matter how much it looks like they are.
checkpoints.criteria: Choose the correct driver for five screws immediately.

checkpoints.title: Drive into plastic
checkpoints.practice:
Printed test block, four holes.

1. Self tapper into a raw hole. Start backwards, drive slowly, stop at snug.
2. Do it again in the second hole and deliberately overdrive it until it strips. We want you to feel it.
3. Third hole: drive it in, take it out, drive it in again. Feel how much weaker it is the second time.
4. Fourth hole: machine screw and nut, and notice how none of this applies.
5. That stripped hole is the point of the checkpoint. Knowing what the moment before it feels like is the actual skill.
checkpoints.criteria: Show controlled tightening and recognize the approach to stripping.

checkpoints.title: Specify your own
checkpoints.practice:
Take something you have built or designed and write down the fasteners it needs.

Type, size, length, and how many. Then go to the drawers and pull exactly that, and no extras.
checkpoints.criteria: Assemble a project using a complete and accurate fastener list.

skills.title: The glue shelf
skills.objective: Choose adhesives, prepare and clamp joints, compare failures, and make a real repair.

checkpoints.title: Pick the right one
checkpoints.practice:
We describe five joints. You pick a glue for each and say why.

Some of them are trick questions where the right answer is a screw, or a printed clip, or not joining them at all.
checkpoints.criteria: Make five suitable adhesive decisions, including recognizing an unsuitable glue repair.

checkpoints.title: Prepare a joint properly
checkpoints.practice:
Two scrap printed pieces.

1. Dry fit and check that they meet along the whole joint.
2. Sand both faces.
3. Wipe both faces clean and let them dry.
4. Work out how you will clamp it before you open the glue.
5. That last one is where people come unstuck. Deciding how to hold it with glue already going off is a bad twenty seconds.
checkpoints.criteria: Prepare surfaces and demonstrate clamping before opening the adhesive.

checkpoints.title: Glue it and break it
checkpoints.practice:
Make two identical joints. One properly, one lazily: no sanding, no cleaning, too much glue, no clamp.

Let both cure fully. Fully means what the bottle says, not what you have time for.

Then break them both and look at the broken faces.
checkpoints.criteria: Compare two broken test joints and explain their different performance.

checkpoints.title: Repair something real
checkpoints.practice:
Find something in the repair box, or a part of your own that has broken.

Choose a glue, prepare it, clamp it, and let it cure properly.

Then use it. Not gently. If it is a handle, hang something off it.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete a repair that withstands its intended load.

skills.title: Drill and deburr
skills.objective: Select drill sizes, locate holes, deburr, countersink, and use the drill press with staff.

checkpoints.title: Pick the size
checkpoints.practice:
We give you three jobs: a screw that passes through, a screw that threads in, and a rod that has to turn freely.

Pick the bit for each from the index and say the number out loud before you touch the work.
checkpoints.criteria: Select three suitable sizes and demonstrate them on scrap.

checkpoints.title: Drill it where you marked it
checkpoints.practice:
Marked, punched, clamped, backed, drilled.

Two holes in a scrap printed part, both to a mark, both the right size.
checkpoints.criteria: Drill two round holes within 0.5 mm of their marked locations.

checkpoints.title: Deburr and countersink
checkpoints.practice:
Every hole you drill from now on gets finished.

1. Deburr both sides. A twist of the deburring tool or a larger bit spun by hand.
2. Countersink where a flat head screw has to sit flush.
3. Check it by sitting a straight edge across the hole. It should not rock.
checkpoints.criteria: Remove burrs and seat a countersunk screw flush.

checkpoints.title: The pillar drill, with us
checkpoints.practice:
Standing with a staff member, every time.

1. Glasses on, sleeves in, hair back, nothing loose.
2. Work clamped to the table. Never held.
3. Speed set for the material, and for plastic that means slow.
4. Down slowly, back out to clear, and never let go while it is turning.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate correct pillar-drill operation with staff beside you.

skills.preparation: Prepare the drawing, measuring tools, suitable scrap, workholding, and required protection. Ask the instructor to approve the tool setup before cutting, drilling, heating, or using adhesives.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: Pillar-drill assessment is performed with staff present.
skills.unlocks: Hand-drill access and staff-supervised use of the pillar drill.

skills.title: Clamp and jig
skills.objective: Choose clamps, rehearse assemblies, and build repeatable, understandable jigs.

checkpoints.title: Clamp four ways
checkpoints.practice:
Same joint, four different clamping setups, using four different methods off the rack.

Then say which one you would actually use and why.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate four secure clamping arrangements without marking the part.

checkpoints.title: The dry run
checkpoints.practice:
Take a real glue job with more than two parts.

Assemble it completely, clamped, with no glue at all. Then take it apart and lay the parts out in the order you will need them.

Only then open the glue.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete a fully prepared dry assembly before gluing.

checkpoints.title: Build a jig
checkpoints.practice:
Make something whose only job is to hold something else.

It can be printed, it can be cut from scrap, it can be a block with two pins in it.

1. Decide what has to be repeatable.
2. Design or build the jig so the part can only sit one way.
3. Make it, then use it five times.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce five matching parts with a jig another person can load.

checkpoints.title: Hang it on the wall
checkpoints.practice:
A jig nobody can find is a jig that gets rebuilt.

1. Write on it what it is for and who made it.
2. Write the sizes it is set for.
3. Hang it on the jig wall on a hook of its own.
checkpoints.criteria: Label and store the jig, then have another person use it.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.

skills.title: Heat set inserts
skills.objective: Test hole sizes, install heat-set inserts, and validate durable threaded assemblies.

checkpoints.title: Set up and test hole
checkpoints.practice:
Print or find the test block from the sheet, with the range of hole sizes on it.

1. Iron up to temperature with the insert tip fitted.
2. Try an insert in each hole cold. Find the one where it starts to enter and then stops.
3. That is your hole size for this printer and this insert. Write it in your notebook.
checkpoints.criteria: Determine a suitable hole size through your own test piece.

checkpoints.title: Sink three straight
checkpoints.practice:
Three inserts into a scrap part.

Check square from two directions while it is still soft. If it is leaning, touch back down and let it correct itself. Do not lever it.
checkpoints.criteria: Install three level, square inserts without displaced plastic.

checkpoints.title: Pull test
checkpoints.practice:
Now find out whether they hold.

1. Screw into each one and tighten to snug.
2. Then keep going on one of them until something gives.
3. Look at what failed. Did the screw strip, or did the insert pull out of the plastic?
4. An insert that pulls out went in too shallow, too cool, or crooked. An insert that stays while the screw strips is a good insert.
checkpoints.criteria: Have at least two inserts pass tightening tests and explain any failure.

checkpoints.title: Put them in something real
checkpoints.practice:
A part you actually want. A case, a bracket, a mount.

Design or choose it with the right hole sizes, print it, and fit the inserts.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate five assembly cycles without degradation.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: Requires the Soldering Licence as well as fastener skills.
skills.unlocks: Use of the insert kit and soldering-iron insert tip.

skills.title: Keep an edge
skills.objective: Inspect tools, clean loaded files, retire damaged tools, and maintain an assigned section.

checkpoints.title: Sort the tired tools
checkpoints.practice:
We put a tray of used tools in front of you.

Sort them into the four states, and give a reason for each one.
checkpoints.criteria: Correctly distinguish tools needing cleaning, sharpening, or retirement.

checkpoints.title: Unload and clean
checkpoints.practice:
Bring the loaded ones back.

1. File card across the file, in the direction of the teeth, not across them.
2. Saw teeth cleared with a brush and a pick where plastic has welded in.
3. Snips wiped and the pivot checked for grit.
4. Wipe steel with an oiled rag if it is going away for a while. Not the cutting edge of anything that touches paint or plastic.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate restored cutting performance after cleaning a file.

checkpoints.title: Retire something
checkpoints.practice:
The hard one, because it feels wasteful.

Find a tool in service that should not be, and take it out of service properly.

1. Tag it with what is wrong.
2. Put it on the staff bench.
3. Tell somebody out loud.
4. Write it on the stock board if it needs replacing.
checkpoints.criteria: Correctly remove a genuinely unserviceable tool from use.

checkpoints.title: Own a section
checkpoints.practice:
Take a section of the tool wall as yours for a month.

Once a week: look at every tool in it, clean what needs it, retire what needs it, report what is missing.
checkpoints.criteria: Maintain the assigned section consistently for four weeks.

skills.title: Fix it instead
skills.objective: Diagnose broken printed parts, reinforce breaks, repair threads, and return usable items.

checkpoints.title: Diagnose five
checkpoints.practice:
Five broken parts out of the box.

For each one: how it broke, why it broke, and whether you would repair it or reprint it.
checkpoints.criteria: Diagnose at least four of five failures, including when reprinting is preferable.

checkpoints.title: Pin a break
checkpoints.practice:
The core structural repair.

1. Line the break up and mark where the pin goes, through both halves.
2. Drill both halves, matched, using the marks. This is where the Drill badge earns its place.
3. Dry fit with the pin in. It should close fully.
4. Epoxy, pin, clamp, cure.
5. The pin can be a piece of filament, a cut off screw, a brass rod, or a paperclip. What matters is that it crosses the break.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a reinforced repair that survives its original loading.

checkpoints.title: Rebuild a thread
checkpoints.practice:
A stripped hole, brought back.

Choose one: a heat set insert, a bigger self tapper, a nut trapped behind, or a plug glued in and re drilled.

Say why you chose it before you do it.
checkpoints.criteria: Restore a screw hole that withstands repeated cycles and tightening.

checkpoints.title: Take on a real one
checkpoints.practice:
Something the workshop actually needs back, or somebody's own broken build.

Diagnose, repair, test, and hand it back with one sentence about why it broke and what you did.

That sentence is not optional. It is how the same part stops breaking.
checkpoints.criteria: Return a functioning item and explain prevention to its owner.

skills.title: The bench test
skills.objective: Make a functional part from a drawing using hand tools, then inspect and hand it over.

checkpoints.title: Read it and plan it
checkpoints.practice:
Before any tool comes off the wall.

1. Read every dimension out loud.
2. Mark the tightest tolerance on the drawing. That feature dictates your order of work.
3. Write your order of operations in your notebook.
4. Say which step is the one that could ruin the part.
checkpoints.criteria: Plan operations around the tightest feature and main failure risk.

checkpoints.title: Make the part
checkpoints.practice:
Work it.

Everything you have learned in this lane is in play: hold it, mark it, cut it, drill it, deburr it, file it, check it.

You may start again on fresh stock once. Everybody who has needed to has still passed.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete the part without staff directing corrections.

checkpoints.title: Inspect it yourself
checkpoints.practice:
Before you hand it over, inspect your own work against the drawing.

Write down every dimension as measured, next to the dimension as drawn.

Include the ones that are out. Especially the ones that are out.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce an inspection report that agrees with independent measurements.

checkpoints.title: Hand it over
checkpoints.practice:
Hand us the part, the drawing and the sheet.

Explain to your instructor the one thing you would do differently if you made a second one.
checkpoints.criteria: Deliver a part within drawing tolerances for assessment by two staff.

skills.title: Slicer basics
skills.objective: Orient models, choose key slicer settings, inspect previews, and submit complete print jobs.

checkpoints.title: Import and orient
checkpoints.practice:
Get the model on the plate and turn it the right way up.

1. Prepare tab. Drag your file onto the plate, or use the Add button
2. Check the size. It is almost never what you assumed
3. Click the model, then LAY ON FACE in the left toolbar. Click the face you want on the plate
4. Look at what is now hanging in the air
5. There is an AUTO ORIENT button too. It is a decent guess, not an answer. Use Lay on Face when you know which face should be down, and you usually do.
checkpoints.criteria: Justify the model's chosen print orientation.

checkpoints.title: The four settings that matter
checkpoints.practice:
Bambu Studio has hundreds. You need four, and they live in the PROCESS panel on the left.

LAYER HEIGHT Set by the preset at the top of the Process panel. 0.20mm Standard is the right answer almost every time. 0.12mm Fine for small detailed things and it will roughly double your time. 0.28mm Draft when you do not care.

WALL LOOPS Strength tab. Default is 2. Go to 3 or 4 for anything that has to survive being used. Walls make a part strong, more than infill does.

SPARSE INFILL DENSITY

Strength tab. This is what Bambu calls infill. 15% is the default and it is fine for most things. Push it up for parts that take load. Do not go to 100% because you think stronger is better.

ENABLE SUPPORT

Support tab. Off by default. Turn it on for real overhangs and pick tree(auto) unless we tell you otherwise. Tree uses less material and comes off easier.
checkpoints.criteria: Select and explain the tradeoffs in the four core settings.

checkpoints.title: Slice and read the preview
checkpoints.practice:
Slicing is not the end of the job. The preview is where you catch things.

1. Hit SLICE PLATE
2. It drops you into the Preview tab
3. Use the slider on the right to cut layers away from the top. Scrub it all the way down and back
4. Look for: parts printing in mid air, walls gone see through thin, supports where you did not want them
5. Read the SLICING RESULTS panel. Total print time and total material
checkpoints.criteria: Find and fix a preview problem, then regenerate the slice.

checkpoints.title: Hand it in
checkpoints.practice:
A job we can print without asking you anything.

1. File named with your name and what it is
2. Print time and material weight from the Slicing Results panel, written down
3. You can say what it is for and how good it needs to be
checkpoints.criteria: Submit a print job that needs no follow-up questions.

skills.title: First print
skills.objective: Choose a suitable first print, check the printer, monitor its first layer, and inspect the result.

checkpoints.title: Pick something sensible
checkpoints.practice:
Your first print is not the thing you most want to make. It is the thing that will teach you the most in under an hour.

Good first prints:

1. Small
2. Flat on the bottom
3. Under an hour
4. No supports
5. Something you actually want
6. If it is bigger than your fist or longer than an hour, it is not this badge.
checkpoints.criteria: Explain why the chosen object is an appropriate first print.

checkpoints.title: Check the machine
checkpoints.practice:
Before anything goes on the plate.

1. Plate is clean and in the right way round
2. Nothing left on it from the last job, including bits you cannot see. Run your hand across it, carefully, when it is cold
3. Filament is loaded and is the colour you actually want
4. Nothing is in the way of the machine moving
checkpoints.criteria: Check the build plate independently and identify a relevant issue.

checkpoints.title: Watch the first layer
checkpoints.practice:
This is the actual skill in this badge.

Stay at the machine. Do not go and do something else.

Watch for:

1. The line coming out smooth and steady, not stringy or gappy
2. It squashing onto the plate, not sitting on top of it like a worm
3. Lines touching each other with no gaps
4. Nothing peeling up at the corners
checkpoints.criteria: Correctly judge whether the first layer should continue.

checkpoints.title: Get it off and look at it
checkpoints.practice:
The job is not done when the printer stops.

1. Wait for the bed to cool. Most parts come off on their own
2. Do not lever it off with anything metal
3. Remove the brim or skirt
4. Look at it properly. Top, bottom, sides
5. Then explain to your instructor one thing that came out well and one thing you would change.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify a real defect in the completed print.

skills.title: Plate and adhesion
skills.objective: Match plates to materials, maintain adhesion, and diagnose warping through controlled tests.

checkpoints.title: Match plate to job
checkpoints.practice:
We give you four jobs: a tall thin part, a wide flat part, a display piece that wants a shiny bottom, and something in a material you have not used.

Pick a plate for each and say why.
checkpoints.criteria: Make four appropriate plate choices and know when to ask staff.

checkpoints.title: Clean it properly
checkpoints.practice:
A plate off the machine, cold.

1. Warm water and dish soap, both sides, with your hands not a scourer.
2. Rinse and dry it fully.
3. Hold it by the edges from here on.
4. Look across the surface into the light. Streaks and rainbows mean it is not clean yet.
5. Water beading up on it means grease. Water running off in a sheet means clean. That is the whole test and it takes two seconds.
checkpoints.criteria: Clean and handle a plate without contaminating its printing surface.

checkpoints.title: Make it fail on purpose
checkpoints.practice:
The checkpoint people remember.

Print a small four corner test twice.

1. Once on a properly cleaned plate.
2. Once after deliberately putting a thumbprint in the middle of the plate.
3. Then compare the two first layers and try to lift each part off while the plate is still warm.
checkpoints.criteria: Compare adhesion behavior and explain the effect of contamination.

checkpoints.title: Rescue a warp
checkpoints.practice:
Take a part that has been lifting at the corners and fix it without changing the model.

Your options, in the order to try them:

1. Clean the plate properly.
2. Add a brim.
3. Close the door or move the machine out of the draught.
4. Change the plate type.
5. Only then, come and talk to us about temperature.
checkpoints.criteria: Print the previously warped part flat using isolated changes.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Independent plate selection and changes, plus use of the glue stick.

skills.title: Know your filament
skills.objective: Select, load, store, diagnose, and dry filament for the intended application.

checkpoints.title: Pick for the job
checkpoints.practice:
Five parts, described by what they have to do.

A phone stand. A hinge that flexes. A bracket for a car. A display model. A wheel for the rover.

Pick a material for each and say what would go wrong with your second choice.
checkpoints.criteria: Give five application-based material choices with reasons.

checkpoints.title: Load and unload
checkpoints.practice:
On a real machine, both directions.

1. Check the spool for a crossed wind and unwind a turn.
2. Cut the end at an angle. A blunt end catches.
3. Load and watch the colour change come through fully before you start.
4. Unload, and put the end through a hole in the spool so it cannot unwind in the bag.
5. Bag it with the desiccant.
6. That last step is the one everybody skips and it is the reason half the failures on this pathway happen.
checkpoints.criteria: Load and unload independently, then store the spool correctly.

checkpoints.title: See wet filament
checkpoints.practice:
We keep a deliberately wet spool for this.

Print the same small test with the wet spool and with a dry one.

Listen while it is printing. The wet one hisses and pops. Then compare the two parts side by side under a light.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify audible and surface evidence of wet filament.

checkpoints.title: Dry one and prove it
checkpoints.practice:
Take a suspect spool, put it in the dryer at the setting on the chart, and print the same test again afterwards.

Write the before and after in your notebook with the drying time.
checkpoints.criteria: Show an improved print after drying and record the settings.

skills.title: Supports and overhangs
skills.objective: Test overhangs, reduce support needs through orientation, and remove supports cleanly.

checkpoints.title: Print the overhang test
checkpoints.practice:
There is a test model on the shelf that steps from 0 to 80 degrees.

Print it with no supports at all, then look at it in raking light.
checkpoints.criteria: Measure the machine's overhang droop and failure angles.

checkpoints.title: Turn the problem away
checkpoints.practice:
We give you three models that all look like they need support.

For each, find an orientation that removes some or all of it.

Show your instructor the preview both ways.
checkpoints.criteria: Eliminate supports for one test part and reduce them for others.

checkpoints.title: Paint supports on
checkpoints.practice:
A model that genuinely needs support somewhere.

1. Turn support on and pick tree(auto).
2. Then use the paint tool to put support only where the part needs it.
3. Slice and compare material and time against supports everywhere.
checkpoints.criteria: Use targeted supports to reduce time and material while retaining printability.

checkpoints.title: Get them off cleanly
checkpoints.practice:
Removal is a hand skill and it is why the Cutting badge is worth having.

1. Break the bulk away by hand where it comes freely.
2. Snips flat against the part for the stubs.
3. A pick or a needle file for what is left in corners.
4. Never a knife pulled toward your hand.
checkpoints.criteria: Remove supports without noticeable scarring or gouging.

skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.

skills.title: Orientation and strength
skills.objective: Evaluate layer-direction strength and choose walls, infill, and orientation for real loads.

checkpoints.title: Break the coupons
checkpoints.practice:
Print the same test hook three ways: flat, on edge, and standing up.

Same settings, same material, same machine.

Then break all three in the rig and record the force or the feel.
checkpoints.criteria: Compare broken test coupons and relate failure to layer direction.

checkpoints.title: Walls versus infill
checkpoints.practice:
Two more coupons.

1. One with 2 wall loops and 40% sparse infill.
2. One with 5 wall loops and 10% sparse infill.
3. Compare material used and print time from the Slicing Results panel before you print. Then break them.
checkpoints.criteria: Explain the strength differences produced by walls and infill.

checkpoints.title: Orient a real job
checkpoints.practice:
Take a functional part somebody actually needs.

1. Say where the load comes from.
2. Say which way it would break.
3. Orient it so the layers resist that.
4. Accept the surface finish you get as a result, and say what you gave up.
checkpoints.criteria: Choose and defend the orientation of a real loaded part.

checkpoints.title: Catch somebody else's
checkpoints.practice:
Look at three jobs in the queue or on the shelf that belong to other people.

Find one that is oriented wrong for what it has to do, and say so to the person, kindly, with the reason.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify and explain a strength-related problem in another print job.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.

skills.title: Print rescue
skills.objective: Read failed prints, identify failure modes, isolate causes, and prove a corrective change.

checkpoints.title: Read the evidence
checkpoints.practice:
Do not clear the plate. Do not scrape anything off. Look first.

1. At what height did it fail
2. What is happening at that height in the model. An overhang, a bridge, a sudden change in area
3. Is the failure on one side or all round
4. Is anything still stuck to the plate
5. Did the printer carry on printing in the air
checkpoints.criteria: Describe where and when a supplied print failed before diagnosing it.

checkpoints.title: Name the failure
checkpoints.practice:
Every common failure in this workshop has a name. Use it.

WARPING Corners lift off the plate. Bottom of the print.

FIRST LAYER FAILURE

Nothing stuck at all, or a mat of dragged lines.

LAYER SHIFT The whole print steps sideways at one height, and everything above is offset.

SPAGHETTI The part came loose and the printer kept extruding into the air.

UNDER EXTRUSION Thin, gappy walls. You can see through the part.

STRINGING Fine hairs between separate parts of the print.

ELEPHANT FOOT First layer squashed out wider than the rest.

SUPPORT FAILURE

Supports fell over or were never there.
checkpoints.criteria: Recognize the failure types assessed without consulting the lesson.

checkpoints.title: Find the cause
checkpoints.practice:
Now the why. Most failures have two or three usual causes and one of them is far more likely than the others.

WARPING Cool draught, dirty plate, no brim, or material choice.

FIRST LAYER Dirty plate, nozzle too far away, model floating above the plate in the slice.

LAYER SHIFT Something hit the print or the gantry. Usually the part came loose, or you left something on the bed.

SPAGHETTI Adhesion. It always starts as the part letting go.

UNDER EXTRUSION

Partial nozzle clog, wet or tangled filament, or the spool snagging.

STRINGING Wet filament, or temperature too high.
checkpoints.criteria: State the single most likely cause before offering alternatives.

checkpoints.title: Fix it and prove it
checkpoints.practice:
A diagnosis you have not tested is still a guess.

1. Change ONE thing
2. Print it again, or print a small test piece rather than the whole six hour job
3. Compare it to the failure
4. Write down what you changed and what happened
checkpoints.criteria: Turn a repeatedly failing print into a success through one explained change.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.

skills.title: Bed and nozzle
skills.objective: Clean build plates, inspect nozzles, clear blockages with staff, and validate printer performance.

checkpoints.title: Clean the plate
checkpoints.practice:
The single highest value thing anybody does to a printer.

1. Plate off the machine and cold
2. Warm water and dish soap. Wash both sides
3. Do not use anything abrasive
4. Dry it properly
5. Handle it by the edges from now on. Your fingers are greasy even when they feel clean
checkpoints.criteria: Show a clean plate and handle it without touching the printing face.

checkpoints.title: Inspect the nozzle
checkpoints.practice:
Cold. Every time.

1. Look at the tip under a light
2. Look for burnt plastic stuck round the outside
3. Look for anything crusted on the silicone sock
4. Check the tip is not visibly rounded or scored
5. Burnt plastic round the nozzle ends up dropped into your print at layer forty.
checkpoints.criteria: Distinguish clean, dirty, and damaged nozzle examples.

checkpoints.title: Clear a blockage
checkpoints.practice:
With us. Every time, even after you have the badge.

1. Heat to the right temperature for the material
2. Push filament through by hand and feel for resistance
3. Cold pull if we tell you to
4. Look at what comes out. The colour and the shape of the tip tells you what was in there
checkpoints.criteria: Clear a blockage alongside staff and explain the material removed.

checkpoints.title: Prove the machine
checkpoints.practice:
Maintenance you have not verified is just fiddling.

1. Run the machine's own calibration or levelling routine
2. Print a small first layer test
3. Look at it. Even lines, no gaps, no transparent patches
4. Log it. Machine, date, what you did
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a consistent test square and record the maintenance.

skills.title: Make a profile
skills.objective: Run controlled print experiments, select settings, and publish reproducible slicer profiles.

checkpoints.title: Run a temperature tower
checkpoints.practice:
Pick a material you actually use.

Print the tower, then examine each block under a light: surface finish, stringing between the arms, and how hard it is to snap the tab off.

Pick your temperature and say why, in terms of what you are trading.
checkpoints.criteria: Choose a temperature from your own tower and explain its tradeoff.

checkpoints.title: One variable at a time
checkpoints.practice:
Choose a problem you actually have. Stringing, weak walls, poor overhangs, rough top surfaces.

1. Write down the problem and how you will measure it.
2. Print a reference with the current profile and keep it.
3. Change one setting. Print again. Label it.
4. Repeat three times.
5. Line them up and compare against the reference.
checkpoints.criteria: Record four labeled tests that isolate one setting.

checkpoints.title: Save it and name it
checkpoints.practice:
Save the profile properly.

1. Name it so somebody else knows what it is for. Material, machine, purpose, your initials.
2. Write what it changes from the workshop default and why, in your notebook and on the profile notes.
3. Never overwrite a workshop profile. Save as.
4. A profile called test3 final REAL helps nobody, including you, in two weeks.
checkpoints.criteria: Save a clearly named profile with usable documentation.

checkpoints.title: Somebody else gets your result
checkpoints.practice:
Hand your profile to another person with a job of their own.

They print with it. You do not stand over them.
checkpoints.criteria: Have another person reproduce the result without further instructions.

skills.title: Colour changes
skills.objective: Plan and run color changes while quantifying and managing purge waste.

checkpoints.title: Pause at layer
checkpoints.practice:
The cheap technique, and often the right one.

1. Find the layer where the colour should change, in the preview.
2. Insert the pause at that layer.
3. Print, and be there for the pause.
4. Swap and purge by hand until the colour is clean, then resume.
5. A nameplate with a contrasting top face is the classic and it costs almost nothing.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a clean color boundary at the chosen layer.

checkpoints.title: Read the purge before you print
checkpoints.practice:
Take a multi colour model and slice it three ways:

1. As designed, all colours.
2. With one colour removed.
3. With the colours grouped so there are fewer changes.
4. Write down the part weight and the purge weight for all three.
checkpoints.criteria: Record the six comparison figures and justify the selected job version.

checkpoints.title: Run a real multi colour job
checkpoints.practice:
Load it, check the spool assignments twice, and run it.

Assignments are where this goes wrong. The slicer's colour one is whichever spool is in slot one, and it does not check whether you agree.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a multi-color part with the intended color placement.

checkpoints.title: Do something with the purge
checkpoints.practice:
The waste is real and you are going to look at it.

1. Weigh the purge from your job.
2. Compare it to the weight of the part.
3. Then either print the purge into something useful, or take it to the scrap station and log it.
checkpoints.criteria: Weigh the part and purge, calculate the ratio, and account for waste.

skills.title: The big one
skills.objective: Plan long prints, divide oversized models, validate joints, and finish seams.

checkpoints.title: Weigh the job
checkpoints.practice:
Before any long print.

1. Get the material figure from the Slicing Results panel.
2. Weigh the spool. An empty spool is a known weight and it is written on the shelf.
3. Subtract, and compare.
4. If it is close, change the spool. Close is not enough over eighteen hours.
checkpoints.criteria: Compare required and available material before authorizing the job.

checkpoints.title: Split a model properly
checkpoints.practice:
Take something too big for the plate and cut it.

1. Choose the seam and say why.
2. Add pins and sockets with clearance.
3. Print a small test of just the joint before you print the whole thing.
4. That joint test is not optional. It is a twenty minute print that saves a twelve hour one.
checkpoints.criteria: Validate a joint that assembles and separates by hand before gluing.

checkpoints.title: Run an overnight
checkpoints.practice: Review the academy long-print procedure with the instructor. Record the approved material, profile, monitoring arrangement, first-layer check, and shutdown response. Only the responsible instructor may authorize continued operation. Inspect the completed or stopped job and explain the result from the log.
checkpoints.criteria: Follow the instructor-approved long-print procedure, record supervision and monitoring, and explain the outcome from evidence.

checkpoints.title: Join it invisibly
checkpoints.practice:
Assemble the big part.

1. Dry fit first, all pieces.
2. Glue the way the Glue badge says: rough, clean, less than you think, clamp.
3. Then fill and sand the seam.
4. Prime it if you are going to paint, because primer shows every seam you missed.
checkpoints.criteria: Finish the joint so a new viewer cannot readily identify the seam.

skills.title: Queue operator

checkpoints.title: Triage a real queue
checkpoints.practice:
Take a full day's queue and sequence it.

Write the running order with a reason against each job. Which machine, what order, and why.

Include at least one job you would not run as submitted.
checkpoints.criteria: Sequence a real queue by material and deadline, rejecting unsuitable work correctly.

checkpoints.title: Reject one, kindly
checkpoints.practice:
A real job, a real person, a real conversation.

Explain what is wrong, what would fix it, and offer to look at it together.
checkpoints.criteria: Explain a rejection so the submitter can fix the job without embarrassment.

checkpoints.title: Run a shift
checkpoints.practice:
A full session as the operator.

1. Check every plate before every job.
2. Start each print and watch each first layer.
3. Log every job: machine, material, who it is for, start and finish.
4. Deal with whatever goes wrong, and write down what it was.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete a shift with accurate logs and correctly returned parts.

checkpoints.title: Own a failure
checkpoints.practice:
Something will fail. It always does.

Take a failure that happened on your shift, diagnose it, tell the owner, and say what you will do differently.

Then reprint it, at the front of the queue, because it was yours.
checkpoints.criteria: Resolve a failed job proactively and deliver a usable replacement.

checkpoints.title: Hand the queue over
checkpoints.practice:
At the end of your shift, hand over to whoever is next.

What is running, what is finishing when, what is waiting, what needs watching, what broke.
checkpoints.criteria: Leave a handover the next operator can use without questions.

skills.title: Circuits without solder
skills.objective: Read breadboard connections, build LED circuits, add controls, and trace faults.

checkpoints.title: Read the board
checkpoints.practice:
A breadboard is not a random grid of holes. It has a pattern and until you can see it, nothing will work.

1. The two long rails down the sides are power. One positive, one negative
2. The short rows in the middle are connected across, five holes at a time
3. The channel down the centre splits left from right. Nothing crosses it
4. Rows are not connected to each other
checkpoints.criteria: Correctly identify whether arbitrary breadboard holes are connected.

checkpoints.title: Light an led
checkpoints.practice:
The first circuit everybody builds.

1. LED into the board. Long leg is positive, and the flat side of the rim is negative
2. Resistor in series with it. Not optional
3. Wire from the positive rail to the LED
4. Wire from the resistor back to the negative rail
5. Check it. Then power it
6. The resistor is what stops the LED burning itself out. An LED with no resistor works brilliantly for about four seconds.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate a working LED circuit and trace its complete current path.

checkpoints.title: Add control
checkpoints.practice:
A circuit that is always on is not doing much.

1. Put a switch or a button in the path
2. Add a second LED on its own resistor
3. Wire them so both are on the same switch
4. Then rewire so only one is
checkpoints.criteria: Build and explain both series and parallel control arrangements.

checkpoints.title: Break it and fix it
checkpoints.practice:
The actual skill.

Somebody else will break your circuit, one wire, while you are not looking. You find it.

1. Look before you touch anything
2. Trace the path
3. Check the easy things first. Power connected, LED the right way round, everything pushed fully in
4. Find it, say what was wrong, then fix it
checkpoints.criteria: Locate an introduced fault by tracing rather than rebuilding everything.

skills.title: The multimeter
skills.objective: Verify a multimeter and use continuity and voltage measurements to diagnose circuits.

checkpoints.title: Prove the meter
checkpoints.practice:
Before any measurement.

1. Black in COM, red in the volts socket.
2. Set to continuity.
3. Touch the probes together. It beeps.
4. Now hold one probe and pinch the other tip. It should not beep, because you are not a wire.
checkpoints.criteria: Check the meter before each session without reminders.

checkpoints.title: Find five breaks
checkpoints.practice:
We give you a board with five faults on it. Broken wires, a wire in the wrong row, a switch that never closes, a dead jumper, a rail that does not reach the end.

Find them all with continuity, power off.
checkpoints.criteria: Locate and explain five faults using measurements.

checkpoints.title: Measure voltage along a circuit
checkpoints.practice:
Power on for this one.

1. Black probe on ground and leave it there.
2. Red probe at the supply rail. Write the number.
3. Red probe after the resistor. Write it.
4. Red probe after the LED. Write it.
5. Then look at your three numbers. They add up, and where the voltage disappears is where the work is being done.
checkpoints.criteria: Record three voltages and account for their distribution across components.

checkpoints.title: Check somebody else's
checkpoints.practice:
Somebody has a circuit that does not work.

Meter it with them. Do not touch their board. Tell them where to put the probes.

Find the fault by measuring and let them fix it.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify another person's fault so they can repair it themselves.

skills.title: Cells and packs
skills.objective: Identify battery types, assess condition, use suitable charging, and understand short-circuit hazards.

checkpoints.title: Name and measure
checkpoints.practice:
Five batteries from the drawer.

For each: what type, what nominal voltage, what it is for, and what the meter says right now.

Then explain to your instructor which ones are usable.
checkpoints.criteria: Correctly name, measure, and assess five supplied cells.

checkpoints.title: Spot the bad one
checkpoints.practice: Use photographs or instructor-controlled, isolated examples to identify swelling, dents, corrosion, and damaged insulation. Explain how to stop use and report a suspect cell. Students do not handle damaged cells.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify damage from safe reference examples and explain how to stop use and report the cell without handling it.

checkpoints.title: Charge one properly
checkpoints.practice: With an instructor present, inspect a suitable undamaged rechargeable cell and confirm the manufacturer-specified charger, connector, settings, and charging location. Observe the charge and follow the approved response to unusual heat, swelling, odor, or noise. Record completion and storage arrangements.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete a correct charge cycle with an unprompted mid-cycle check.

checkpoints.title: Short one on purpose
checkpoints.practice: Use a circuit simulation or an instructor-selected recording to investigate a short circuit. Explain how low resistance can produce excessive current and heat, and how protection reduces the risk. Do not deliberately short, heat, or touch a warming battery.
checkpoints.criteria: Explain short-circuit current, heating, and protective measures using a simulation or recording; no live battery fault demonstration.

skills.title: Buttons and buzzers
skills.objective: Build switch, buzzer, and LED circuits with understandable input and output behavior.

checkpoints.title: The button that actually works
checkpoints.practice:
One LED, one resistor, one tactile button.

1. Straddle the button across the centre channel.
2. Wire it so the LED lights only while the button is held.
3. Prove it with the meter, power off: continuity across your two chosen legs only when pressed.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate correct momentary LED control and explain switch connections.

checkpoints.title: Two inputs, two outputs
checkpoints.practice:
Build a circuit with two buttons and two outputs, and give them different jobs.

1. One button lights an LED.
2. The other sounds a buzzer.
3. Then rewire so both buttons together are needed for one of them.
4. That last one is an AND, and you have just built logic out of two switches.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate all three specified behaviors and identify series and parallel arrangements.

checkpoints.title: Make it a thing
checkpoints.practice:
A small finished circuit with a purpose. Not a demo, a thing.

A doorbell. A quiz buzzer. A drawer alarm using a normally closed switch. A morse key.

It has to survive being handed to somebody who did not build it.
checkpoints.criteria: Build a device whose function another person can infer.

checkpoints.title: Draw it afterwards
checkpoints.practice:
Sketch your circuit on paper: what connects to what.

It does not have to be a proper schematic yet. That is the next badge but one. It has to be readable.
checkpoints.criteria: Draw the circuit accurately enough to rebuild it later.

skills.title: Sense the room
skills.objective: Characterize sensors, build voltage dividers, set thresholds, and test unreliable conditions.

checkpoints.title: Measure a sensor's range
checkpoints.practice:
Take an LDR and a meter.

1. Measure its resistance in the room as it is. Write it down.
2. Cover it with your hand. Write it down.
3. Shine a torch on it. Write it down.
4. Now pick the number that means dark for this room.
checkpoints.criteria: Record three sensor measurements and justify a threshold.

checkpoints.title: Build a divider
checkpoints.practice:
A sensor on its own gives resistance. A circuit needs voltage.

1. Fixed resistor from the positive rail to a point.
2. The LDR from that point to ground.
3. Measure the voltage at the point between them, in light and in dark.
4. That is a voltage divider and it is the most reused circuit in electronics. You will meet it again in every project you ever build.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate the divider's response to light and explain its direction.

checkpoints.title: Make it do something
checkpoints.practice:
Use one sensor to trigger one output.

It can be as simple as a transistor switching an LED, or as involved as a comparator.

A nightlight, a drawer alarm with a reed switch, a tilt alarm on a box.
checkpoints.criteria: Trigger the intended response reliably in the actual operating location.

checkpoints.title: Fool your own sensor
checkpoints.practice:
Now try to break it.

1. Move it to a different room or a different light.
2. Shade it, warm it, tap it.
3. Find the situation where it gets it wrong.
4. Every sensor has one. Knowing yours is the difference between a demo and a device.
checkpoints.criteria: Describe failure conditions and a suitable response to each.

skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.

skills.title: Ohm's law by hand
skills.objective: Read resistor codes, predict current, select values, and check component limits.

checkpoints.title: Read the bands
checkpoints.practice:
Ten resistors out of the cabinet, no packets.

Read each one from the bands, then check it with the meter.
checkpoints.criteria: Read at least eight of ten codes correctly, then verify all ten.

checkpoints.title: Predict then measure
checkpoints.practice:
Build an LED circuit with a resistor you chose by calculation.

1. Write down the current you expect, before you power it.
2. Power it and measure the actual current.
3. Compare.
4. Being within about twenty percent is a pass. Real components are not exact and neither is the LED's drop.
checkpoints.criteria: Compare predicted and measured results and explain any difference.

checkpoints.title: Pick for three different supplies
checkpoints.practice:
The same LED, three supplies: 3.3 volts, 5 volts, 9 volts.

Work out the resistor for each and pick a real value from the cabinet.

Then build all three and compare the brightness.
checkpoints.criteria: Choose suitable resistors for three supplies and verify similar LED brightness.

checkpoints.title: Work out what is too much
checkpoints.practice:
Now the safety half.

1. Take one of your circuits and work out the power in the resistor.
2. Then work out what would happen with no resistor at all.
3. Then explain to your instructor what would happen with a resistor ten times too small.
4. You do not have to build the last two. That is the point of being able to do the arithmetic.
checkpoints.criteria: Use numbers to explain the consequences of excessive LED current.

skills.title: Read a diagram
skills.objective: Recognize schematic symbols, follow branches, build from diagrams, and document circuits.

checkpoints.title: Know the symbols
checkpoints.practice:
The ones you actually need:

Resistor

1. Battery or power
2. Ground

4. LED

1. Switch or button
2. Capacitor
3. Motor
4. A chip, drawn as a box with numbered legs
checkpoints.criteria: Draw and name all eight assessed symbols from memory.

checkpoints.title: Trace the path
checkpoints.practice:
Follow the current with your finger.

1. Start at positive
2. Follow the line
3. Every time it branches, note it
4. End at ground
5. Do it again for every branch
6. Watch for dots. A dot means joined. No dot means one wire is passing over the other.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify series and parallel relationships in a three-branch schematic.

checkpoints.title: Build from paper
checkpoints.practice:
Now do it for real.

1. Take a schematic you have not built
2. Build it on the breadboard
3. Do not look at a photo of a finished one. The schematic is the instruction
4. Your layout will look nothing like anybody else's. That is correct.
checkpoints.criteria: Build a working circuit from its diagram using your own physical layout.

checkpoints.title: Draw your own
checkpoints.practice:
The other direction, and the harder one.

1. Build something on the breadboard
2. Draw its schematic
3. Hand the drawing to somebody else
4. They build it from your drawing alone
checkpoints.criteria: Create a diagram another person can build from without questions.

skills.title: Wire and connectors
skills.objective: Strip, crimp, insulate, test, and organize reliable wiring and connectors.

checkpoints.title: Strip ten clean
checkpoints.practice:
Ten strips, five solid and five stranded, at 5mm.

Look at every one under the light.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce ten clean wire strips without damaged strands or insulation.

checkpoints.title: Crimp and pull
checkpoints.practice:
Dupont pins, the ones the breadboard jumpers use.

1. Strip to the right length.
2. Set the pin in the right slot of the tool.
3. Wings onto the copper, second wings onto the insulation.
4. Crimp, then pull it hard.
5. Every crimp gets pulled. Every one. A crimp that comes off in your hand on the bench was going to come off in a rover at speed.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce five consecutive crimps that pass inspection and pull tests.

checkpoints.title: Make a real lead
checkpoints.practice:
A lead you actually need, to the length you actually need it.

1. Measure the route, add a little for a repair, and cut.
2. Heat shrink on first.
3. Ends made and tested.
4. Shrink it down with the heat gun, not a lighter.
checkpoints.criteria: Make a correctly fitted lead with secure ends and neat insulation.

checkpoints.title: Make a loom
checkpoints.practice:
Three or more wires going the same way, bundled and dressed.

1. Same length, routed together, no crossing.
2. Bundled with sleeving, spiral wrap or ties.
3. Fanned out neatly at each end.
4. Strain relieved so a pull lands on the bundle, not the joints.
checkpoints.criteria: Create an organized loom in which every wire is traceable.

skills.title: Soldering licence
skills.objective: Prepare a soldering station, maintain the tip, make sound joints, and shut down correctly.

checkpoints.title: Set up the station
checkpoints.practice:
1. Iron in the stand, cord clear of the edge
2. Sponge damp. Squeeze it out. Dripping wet is wrong
3. Brass wool within reach
4. Solder unspooled about 20cm
5. Board in the vise, not in your hand
checkpoints.criteria: Arrange the station so supplies are reachable without crossing the iron.

checkpoints.title: Tin the tip
checkpoints.practice:
A bare tip does not pass heat. Solder sticks to solder, not to dirty metal.

1. Let it come up to temperature
2. Wipe once on the damp sponge
3. Touch solder to the tip until it coats
4. Wipe again
checkpoints.criteria: Maintain an evenly tinned tip without contamination or excess solder.

checkpoints.title: Three good joints
checkpoints.practice:
Practice board. Not your project. Nobody starts on the real thing.

The order matters:

1. Touch the iron to the pad AND the wire at the same time
2. Count two
3. Feed solder into the joint, not onto the iron
4. Count one
5. Solder away, then iron away
6. Do not move the wire while it sets
checkpoints.criteria: Make three consecutive acceptable joints that pass mechanical checks.

checkpoints.title: A real component
checkpoints.practice:
Now it counts.

1. Check the part goes in the right way round. Ask if you are not sure
2. Bend the legs so it sits flat
3. Solder one leg only
4. Check it is sitting straight. Fix it now if it is not
5. Solder the rest
6. Trim the legs above the joint, not into it
checkpoints.criteria: Install a component with sound joints, no bridges, and trimmed leads.

checkpoints.title: Shut down
checkpoints.practice:
The last one, and the one people forget.

1. Tip wiped and re tinned before it cools
2. Iron off and in the stand
3. Solder wound back on the spool
4. Offcuts in the bin, not on the floor
5. Bench wiped
6. Hands washed
checkpoints.criteria: Restore the station to a safe, ready condition.

skills.guidance: Licence. Assessments include station setup and shutdown.

skills.title: Rework and rescue
skills.objective: Remove solder bridges and components, replace joints, and repair damaged connections.

checkpoints.title: Clear a bridge
checkpoints.practice:
Make a bridge between two pads on purpose. Then clear it.

1. Flux on the bridge.
2. Wick on top.
3. Iron on the wick, pressing it into the joint.
4. Watch the solder climb into the braid, then lift both together.
checkpoints.criteria: Remove a bridge while leaving both pads undamaged.

checkpoints.title: Remove a through hole part
checkpoints.practice:
A resistor or a header pin off a scrap board.

Add fresh solder first, then wick or pump each leg, then walk the part out.

Then clean the holes so a new part could go in.
checkpoints.criteria: Remove a through-hole part with clear holes and intact board material.

checkpoints.title: Replace it with a good joint
checkpoints.practice:
Put a new part in the holes you just cleared and solder it properly.

The finished joint should be indistinguishable from one that was never touched.
checkpoints.criteria: Install the replacement with sound joints and intact pads.

checkpoints.title: Rescue a lifted pad
checkpoints.practice:
With us. We will provide a board with a lifted pad, or your own if you have just made one.

1. Look at where the track goes and find the next point on it.
2. Scrape a little of the track back to bare copper.
3. Solder a fine wire from the component leg to that point.
4. Secure the wire so it cannot flex.
checkpoints.criteria: Restore circuit operation with a mechanically secure pad repair.

skills.title: Breadboard to protoboard
skills.objective: Translate breadboard circuits into documented, tested, housed permanent boards.

checkpoints.title: Draw the layout
checkpoints.practice:
Take a circuit you already have working on a breadboard.

Draw it on squared paper, hole for hole.

1. Every component in its holes.
2. Every link wire.
3. Every track cut marked clearly, in a different colour.
4. The board outline and which way up it goes.
checkpoints.criteria: Provide a layout another person could build without the schematic.

checkpoints.title: Cut and verify the tracks
checkpoints.practice:
Cut every track break with the track cutter.

Then meter every single one: continuity should stop where you cut and continue where you did not.

Look at the copper side under the light for whiskers of copper bridging a cut.
checkpoints.criteria: Verify every track cut electrically and correct incomplete cuts.

checkpoints.title: Build it and meter it
checkpoints.practice:
Low parts first, sockets, tall parts last.

Solder, trim, inspect.

Then meter the finished board against the schematic before it goes anywhere near power.
checkpoints.criteria: Check all board connections against the schematic before power.

checkpoints.title: Power it and house it
checkpoints.practice:
First power on with us, current limited if the supply can do it.

Then put it in something. A printed case, a box, anything that means it can live on a shelf and be used.

1. Mounting holes or standoffs so the board is not resting on its legs.
2. Strain relief on anything leaving the box.
3. A label saying what it is and who made it.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate a functioning, housed circuit that tolerates normal handling.

skills.title: Fault finding
skills.objective: Describe faults precisely, narrow the circuit systematically, and verify durable repairs.

checkpoints.title: Describe it precisely
checkpoints.practice:
We hand you a faulted board.

Before touching a meter, write down:

1. What it should do.
2. What it actually does, in detail.
3. What that rules out already.
checkpoints.criteria: Describe the fault well enough for another person to reproduce it.

checkpoints.title: Halve it
checkpoints.practice:
Now find it.

Every measurement you take, say out loud what you expect to see and what each possible answer would mean.

Keep a running list of what is eliminated.
checkpoints.criteria: Find the fault through a documented sequence of narrowing measurements.

checkpoints.title: Fix it and prove it
checkpoints.practice:
Repair it properly. Not a temporary bodge unless you say out loud that it is one.

Then prove it works, and prove it stays working: leave it running, tap it, flex the leads, warm it with a hand.
checkpoints.criteria: Prove the repair withstands the conditions that previously caused failure.

checkpoints.title: Find one you cannot see
checkpoints.practice:
The hard one. An intermittent fault, planted by us.

It works, then it does not, then it does.

Intermittents are almost always mechanical: a joint, a connector, a wire broken inside its insulation, a component with a cracked leg.
checkpoints.criteria: Locate an intermittent fault and explain its triggering condition.

skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
