skills.title: Build it twice
skills.objective: Specify an original circuit, prototype it, build a permanent version, and document a handover.

checkpoints.title: Specify and design
checkpoints.practice:
A written specification of behaviour, and a schematic you drew.

Every component value chosen by you, with the arithmetic in your notebook.

Bring both before you build anything.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a complete schematic and justify every component value.

checkpoints.title: Prove it on the breadboard
checkpoints.practice:
Build it, and test it against your written behaviour list, item by item.

Tick each behaviour off when it works. Fix what does not.

Then try to break it: low battery, wrong input, a button held down forever.
checkpoints.criteria: Verify every planned behavior and document at least two failure conditions.

checkpoints.title: Build the keeper
checkpoints.practice:
Layout drawn, tracks cut and verified, built low parts first, metered against the schematic before power.

Then housed properly, with strain relief and a label.
checkpoints.criteria: Build a working permanent circuit or diagnose startup faults methodically.

checkpoints.title: Give it away
checkpoints.practice:
Hand it to the person whose problem it solves.

Show them once, then leave it with them for a week.

Then go back and ask what is wrong with it.
checkpoints.criteria: Have the recipient use it for a week and record revision ideas.

checkpoints.title: Write it up
checkpoints.practice:
One document, on paper or in the workshop folder.

1. Schematic.
2. Layout drawing.
3. Parts list with values.
4. One paragraph on how it works, written so somebody who has done Buttons and Buzzers could follow it.
checkpoints.criteria: Provide documentation sufficient for another person to build a second unit.

skills.title: Drive an atlas
skills.objective: Navigate Atlas menus, recover from screens, use tools, and guide another user.

checkpoints.title: Open every door
checkpoints.practice:
Go into all seven, one at a time, and come back out of each with the dial rather than the switch.

In each one, find one thing you did not know was there.
checkpoints.criteria: Name all seven menu doors and describe their purposes.

checkpoints.title: Get out of everything
checkpoints.practice:
The skill that stops people getting stuck.

Go three levels deep into anything, then get back to the main menu with the dial alone.

Then do it from inside a game, which is the one people panic in.
checkpoints.criteria: Return from screens without switching off or guessing the menu depth.

checkpoints.title: Play something properly
checkpoints.practice:
Open Games and play Mouse until you clear level one.

Then find and open one Toy and one Tool, and say what each is for.
checkpoints.criteria: Achieve the specified first-level result and identify a useful tool.

checkpoints.title: Hand it to somebody else
checkpoints.practice:
Give it to somebody who has never held one and get them to the games menu.

You may talk. You may not take it back.
checkpoints.criteria: Guide another person who can then navigate back independently.

skills.title: Flash from a browser
skills.objective: Check USB data connections, flash compatible firmware, and recover interrupted installations.

checkpoints.title: Prove the cable
checkpoints.practice:
Before anything else.

1. Take a cable and plug a board in.
2. If the site cannot see it, take a marked cable from the drawer and try again.
3. Then find a charge only cable in the box and see it fail, so you know what that looks like.
4. Half the flashing problems in the world are this.
checkpoints.criteria: Distinguish data-capable cables from charge-only cables by testing.

checkpoints.title: Flash a board
checkpoints.practice:
A spare board, not somebody's finished device.

Pick the firmware, read the name twice, flash it, wait for done.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete a flash and demonstrate the installed firmware booting.

checkpoints.title: Flash something else
checkpoints.practice:
A different device. A Pioneer board, or a WLED controller.

The process is the same and the firmware is not. Reading which is which is the skill.
checkpoints.criteria: Match and install the correct firmware on another board.

checkpoints.title: Recover a half flashed board
checkpoints.practice:
We will interrupt one on purpose.

It will not boot. That is expected.

Unplug, replug, flash again from the start, and bring it back.
checkpoints.criteria: Recover an interrupted flash on an apparently unresponsive board.

skills.title: Charge and care
skills.objective: Read Atlas status, charge and track runtime, care for a loaner, and report faults clearly.

checkpoints.title: Read its state
checkpoints.practice:
Find, on the device:

1. The battery indicator and what it is telling you.
2. The charging symbol, with a lead in.
3. The firmware version, in Settings.
4. How to get back to the menu from anywhere.
checkpoints.criteria: Report charge, firmware version, and unusual behavior in one concise description.

checkpoints.title: A full charge cycle
checkpoints.practice:
Run it down to the low warning, then charge it fully, and note how long it took.

Write the number in your notebook. Then you know what a healthy one looks like, and you will notice when yours is not.
checkpoints.criteria: Record a charging time and estimate practical runtime.

checkpoints.title: Live with one
checkpoints.practice:
Sign one out and take it home for two weeks.

Bring it back charged, undamaged, and with the case screws still tight.

Use it. A device that comes back unused has not been looked after, it has been avoided.
checkpoints.criteria: Keep an Atlas charged, working, and in use for two weeks.

checkpoints.title: Spot a problem
checkpoints.practice:
Somewhere in these two weeks, or on a workshop unit, find something wrong and report it.

A loose switch, a screw backing out, a screen that flickers, a charge that does not hold.

Report it with what you observed, not what you think it is.
checkpoints.criteria: Report an actual fault with enough detail to reproduce it.

skills.title: Join a screening
skills.objective: Join, navigate, host, and recommend synchronized Atlas Library screenings.

checkpoints.title: Find and join
checkpoints.practice:
Ecosystem, Library, join whatever is running.

Watch a minute. Then leave properly and rejoin.
checkpoints.criteria: Join, leave, and rejoin without disrupting the group.

checkpoints.title: Drive the transport
checkpoints.practice:
On your own screen: pause, scrub back, jump a chapter, come back to where the room is.

Find out what the dial does at each level of press and hold.
checkpoints.criteria: Navigate a reel and return to the live position confidently.

checkpoints.title: Host one
checkpoints.practice:
Start a screening for the room.

1. Check nothing is running.
2. Ask the room what they fancy, or pick something short.
3. Say what it is and how long it is.
4. Stay for it.
checkpoints.criteria: Host a screening joined independently by at least two others.

checkpoints.title: Know the shelf
checkpoints.practice:
Look through what is actually on the Library.

Pick three you have never heard of and watch a few minutes of each.

Then tell somebody about one of them.
checkpoints.criteria: Recommend a Library item with a clear reason.

skills.title: Meet the kit
skills.objective: Identify Atlas kit components, handle the cell responsibly, and inspect printed enclosure parts.

checkpoints.title: Name everything
checkpoints.practice: Lay the kit out and give us the tour yourself.
checkpoints.criteria: Name all five parts and explain their functions without the sheet.

checkpoints.title: Respect the cell
checkpoints.practice:
The battery rules:

1. The leads never touch each other. Tape the bare ends until the moment you solder them.
2. Nothing sharp near it, nothing hot on it, no bending it.
3. If a cell is swollen, dented or smells sweet, it goes to staff. Not in the bin. To us.
4. It rests on the bench, never on the floor and never in a pocket.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate appropriate cell handling without reminders.

checkpoints.title: Check the print
checkpoints.practice:
The case came off a printer in this workshop. Printers have bad days.

Look yours over:

1. Both halves sit flat against each other with no rocking.
2. The screw holes are clear and the screws start by hand.
3. The switch opening and the dial opening are clean.
4. Nothing is cracked, lifted or stringy inside.
5. If something is off, say so now. A case problem is a five minute reprint today and a broken Atlas next week.
checkpoints.criteria: Test-fit case halves and inspect openings before fitting electronics.

skills.title: The power badge
skills.objective: Plan the Atlas power wiring, verify polarity, make joints, and obtain staff inspection.

checkpoints.title: Dry run
checkpoints.practice:
Nothing hot yet.

1. Route the leads the way they will lie in the case.
2. Cut to length with slack for one repair. Not a coil of spare, not banjo string tight.
3. Show your instructor where each end lands and which way the switch faces so you can reach it through the case opening.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete the wiring layout before heating the iron.

checkpoints.title: Polarity, out loud
checkpoints.practice:
Point at the plus pad. Point at the minus pad. Point at the red lead. Point at the black lead.

Say what happens if you swap them.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify and state the correct polarity before proceeding.

checkpoints.title: Make the joints
checkpoints.practice:
Tape the lead you are not working on so it cannot wander.

1. Tin the pad, tin the wire.
2. Bring them together with the iron. Two seconds, shiny, a small hill not a ball.
3. The switch legs get the same care as the board pads.
4. Strain relief. The leads are fixed so a tug pulls on the case, not on your joints.
checkpoints.criteria: Inspect all three joints and redo defects before staff review.

checkpoints.title: The staff check
checkpoints.practice:
Nobody powers a first build alone. Not because we do not trust you. Because that is the rule for everyone, including us.

We check polarity, we check the joints, we check the switch, and then you flick it on for the first time in front of us.
checkpoints.criteria: Pass the staff check for correct on and off behavior.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: Staff inspect the power assembly before the build proceeds.

skills.title: First boot
skills.objective: Fit the Atlas screen, install firmware, and verify the first complete boot.

checkpoints.title: Seat the screen
checkpoints.practice:
1. Line the screen up square to its place.
2. Ease it in evenly. Watch it go, not your thumbs.
3. Look across it edge on. Level, fully home, no lean.
checkpoints.criteria: Fit the screen straight without using force.

checkpoints.title: Flash it
checkpoints.practice:
1. Cable to the bench computer.
2. installatlas dot com in the browser.
3. Pick Atlas, press flash, and do not unplug until it says done.
4. The progress bar is real. Pulling the cable mid flash does not brick the board forever, but it does mean starting again, so let it finish.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete firmware installation without disturbing the connection.

checkpoints.title: The first boot
checkpoints.practice:
Switch on.

The boot banner comes up, then the face. Turn the dial. Press it. Hold it. Find the menu.
checkpoints.criteria: Independently start the device, open a function, and return to the menu.

skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.

skills.title: Close the box
skills.objective: Arrange internal parts, fasten the enclosure, and test the finished Atlas as a product.

checkpoints.title: Dress the inside
checkpoints.practice: With power disconnected, arrange the battery, board, and leads in their intended locations using the approved kit instructions. Test the lid without screws. If it needs pressure, stop and correct the obstruction before proceeding.
checkpoints.criteria: Close the lid without pressure while all internal parts remain secure.

checkpoints.title: Screw it shut
checkpoints.practice: Select the correct driver and start each screw by hand. Tighten evenly until secure, without forcing the plastic threads. Ask the instructor to inspect the closure before powering the device.
checkpoints.criteria: Tighten all screws correctly without stripping them.

checkpoints.title: The product test
checkpoints.practice: Switch on through the case. Dial, press, hold. Charge port reachable. Nothing rattles. The switch clicks with a clean edge to it.
checkpoints.criteria: Pass the finished-device test without unresolved qualifications or faults.

skills.title: Your atlas
skills.objective: Demonstrate the completed Atlas, use the Library, and complete the required game milestone.

checkpoints.title: The tour, given
checkpoints.practice: Show a friend, a parent or a staff member around the whole menu. Every door, one sentence each.
checkpoints.criteria: Give a complete device tour and explain every function shown.

checkpoints.title: The library visit
checkpoints.practice: Go to Ecosystem, open Library, and join whatever is playing on the workshop Library, or start something.
checkpoints.criteria: Watch a Library film on the finished device and leave appropriately.

checkpoints.title: First cheese
checkpoints.practice: Open Mouse. Watch him die. Fix it.
checkpoints.criteria: Achieve the required PERFECT result on the first level.

skills.title: Flash crew
skills.objective: Track firmware versions, update batches, diagnose flashing failures, and guide owners.

checkpoints.title: Know what is current
checkpoints.practice:
Find the current firmware version, read the release notes, and be able to say what changed since the last one in two sentences.

Then check three workshop units and say which need updating.
checkpoints.criteria: Know the current version and correctly check three devices.

checkpoints.title: Flash a batch
checkpoints.practice:
Six units or more, logged properly.

1. Version before, in the log.
2. Flash, wait for done.
3. Boot and check the thing that changed.
4. Version after, in the log.
5. Anything that misbehaved, labelled and set aside.
checkpoints.criteria: Flash a batch with every boot verified and each unit logged.

checkpoints.title: Rescue one
checkpoints.practice:
A unit that will not boot after a flash, or one that arrives half written.

Work through it: cable, port, browser, firmware choice, and only then the hardware.

Do not open a case until you have exhausted the flashing side.
checkpoints.criteria: Recover a device or correctly escalate a hardware fault.

checkpoints.title: Do it for somebody, with them
checkpoints.practice:
Somebody else's device, with them standing there.

1. Ask permission and say what will happen.
2. Tell them their badges and progress are safe, and mean it.
3. Let them press the button.
4. Boot it together.
checkpoints.criteria: Explain an owner's update while letting the owner perform the action.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.

skills.title: The repair bench
skills.objective: Diagnose and repair Atlas screens, switches, cells, and common build faults.

checkpoints.title: Diagnose five without opening
checkpoints.practice:
Five units with five faults, and a description from each owner.

Say what you think is wrong and how confident you are, before any screws come out.
checkpoints.criteria: Correctly diagnose at least four of five devices before opening them.

checkpoints.title: Screen and switch
checkpoints.practice:
The two most common bench jobs.

1. Reseat a screen, then replace one properly.
2. Test a switch line with the meter, find the bad joint, reflow it.
3. Close both units and test them fully.
checkpoints.criteria: Return repaired screen and switch units fully assembled and working.

checkpoints.title: Replace a cell
checkpoints.practice:
With a staff member, the first time.

1. Meter the old cell and record why it is being replaced.
2. Old cell to the battery bin, correctly, taped.
3. New cell in, polarity checked out loud, leads dressed, strain relieved.
4. Staff check before power on. Same rule as build day, forever.
checkpoints.criteria: Replace a cell and confirm operation plus overnight charge retention.

checkpoints.title: Run the bench for a week
checkpoints.practice:
Take whatever comes in for a week.

Log everything. Return everything tested. Escalate what should be escalated.

At the end, explain to your instructor which fault came up most and what you would change about the build to prevent it.
checkpoints.criteria: Account for every repair during a week and report a useful build observation.

skills.preparation: Confirm the exact hardware, pinout, voltage, current limits, and manufacturer instructions. Disconnect power before assembly. An instructor checks wiring and battery arrangements before first power-up.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: Battery replacement remains governed by the full lesson and staff assessment.
skills.unlocks: The Atlas repair bench, spare parts, and assigned repair bookings.

skills.title: The custom case
skills.objective: Measure Atlas internals, test critical interfaces, and publish a custom printed enclosure.

checkpoints.title: Measure the insides
checkpoints.practice:
Every internal part, measured by you, written down.

1. Board outline, thickness, and the position of every mounting hole.
2. Screen module: outline, active area, and where the active area sits within the outline.
3. Cell: length, width, thickness, and lead exit.
4. Switch: body, the panel cutout it needs, and the throw.
checkpoints.criteria: Record a complete, independently measured internal dimension sheet.

checkpoints.title: Test sections first
checkpoints.practice:
Three small prints before any full case:

1. The screen window, with the screen behind it.
2. The switch opening, with the switch clicked in.
3. One corner with a screw boss and an insert.
4. Each one is a twenty minute print. Each one saves a four hour one.
checkpoints.criteria: Make the three test sections fit within two attempts each.

checkpoints.title: Print and assemble
checkpoints.practice:
The whole case, designed for the machine, printed without supports if you can manage it.

Assemble your Atlas into it fully.

Then run the Close The Box product test again: switch, dial, charge port, shake, and hand it to a stranger.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce an assembled case meeting the standard product test.

checkpoints.title: Put it in the library
checkpoints.practice:
Make the design available.

1. Fix whatever version one taught you.
2. Name the files so somebody knows what they are and which way up they print.
3. Write a one page note: print settings, orientation, what fasteners it needs, what it fits.
4. Put it in the workshop case library.
checkpoints.criteria: Have another builder print and use the case without assistance.

skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.

skills.title: Custom firmware
skills.objective: Build Atlas firmware, add a complete menu mode, and validate it on real devices.

checkpoints.title: Build it unchanged
checkpoints.practice:
Before you write a line.

1. Get the firmware onto a build machine.
2. Build it with the board settings exactly as they are written down. They are not negotiable and getting them wrong wastes an afternoon.
3. Flash your own build to your own Atlas.
4. Confirm it boots and behaves identically to a workshop unit.
checkpoints.criteria: Run an unchanged local build that behaves like the standard firmware.

checkpoints.title: Change one visible thing
checkpoints.practice:
Something small and obvious. A string, a menu label, a delay.

Build, flash, and see it on the hardware.

Then put it back and build again, so you know you can.
checkpoints.criteria: Deploy a visible change to hardware, then revert it successfully.

checkpoints.title: Get on the menu
checkpoints.practice:
An empty mode. A screen that says its own name and exits on a held dial.

That is all. It does nothing else yet.

This is the checkpoint where you learn how the menu, the input and the exit all work, and it is worth more than it looks.
checkpoints.criteria: Create a mode that opens, displays, and exits reliably.

checkpoints.title: Make it worth being there
checkpoints.practice:
Now build the actual thing.

1. Keep the scope small enough to finish. One good idea, done properly.
2. Design for the screen: 128 pixels, black and white, one dial.
3. Use Eddy for the parts that are typing and do the thinking yourself.
4. Test on hardware constantly. The preview lies about timing and the hardware does not.
checkpoints.criteria: Deliver a mode that works well on the device.

checkpoints.title: Survive the soak
checkpoints.practice:
The last one, and the one that separates a demo from firmware.

1. Leave it running for an hour and come back.
2. Start it and exit it fifty times.
3. Exit it at every awkward moment you can find.
4. Then go through the whole rest of the menu and check nothing else broke.
5. Then hand your Atlas to three people and let them use it while you say nothing.
checkpoints.criteria: Pass stability testing, preserve existing functions, and observe three independent users.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: Publication depends on staff review and a hardware stability test.

skills.title: First pack
skills.objective: Create, deploy, test, and revise a small Atlas content pack.

checkpoints.title: The smallest thing
checkpoints.practice: Make a pack with at least five entries. Jokes, questions, fortunes, whatever it is.
checkpoints.criteria: Deploy a pack another person can use without explanation.

checkpoints.title: The screen is small on purpose
checkpoints.practice: Go back into your pack and fix the line that is too long. There is always one.
checkpoints.criteria: Verify every line reads cleanly on the physical screen.

checkpoints.title: Version two
checkpoints.practice: Change your pack based on what the first person said, and send it again.
checkpoints.criteria: Observe a user, make a useful revision, and deploy it again.

skills.title: Write for a small screen
skills.objective: Edit concise screen text, improve opening words, and review readability on hardware.

checkpoints.title: Find your own long line
checkpoints.practice:
Open a pack you already made.

Send it to a device and read every screen on the device.

Find every line that breaks badly, crowds, or makes you stumble reading it aloud.

There will be more than you expect.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify at least five readability problems on the actual device.

checkpoints.title: Cut a third
checkpoints.practice:
Take one section of a pack and remove a third of the words without losing anything that matters.

Keep both versions.

Then read both aloud, on the device, to somebody else.
checkpoints.criteria: Reduce the text by a third while improving its effect.

checkpoints.title: Three words first
checkpoints.practice:
Go through every screen in a pack and make sure the first three words say what it is.

Not a title. The actual first three words of the actual text.
checkpoints.criteria: Make every screen understandable during a quick scroll.

checkpoints.title: Fix somebody else's
checkpoints.practice:
With their permission, take a pack somebody else made and edit it for the screen.

Change nothing about what it says. Only how it reads.

Then show them both and let them choose.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce an edit another creator prefers and can explain.

skills.title: Pixels and faces
skills.objective: Draw readable monochrome sprites and images for a 128 by 64 pixel display.

checkpoints.title: Silhouette test
checkpoints.practice:
Draw five objects, at real size, as solid black shapes with no interior detail at all.

A rocket. A cat. A key. A house. Something of your choosing.

Then show them to somebody without saying what they are.
checkpoints.criteria: Have viewers identify at least four of five silhouettes.

checkpoints.title: One face, four moods
checkpoints.practice:
One small face, drawn four times.

Happy, sad, angry, surprised.

You are allowed to change as few pixels as possible between them. Try to do it with two.
checkpoints.criteria: Make four facial expressions readable and explain the important pixels.

checkpoints.title: A full screen
checkpoints.practice:
Use the whole 128 by 64 for one image that says something.

1. One clear subject.
2. Space around it.
3. Contrast that survives at arm's length.
4. Dithering only where an area is big enough to hold it.
checkpoints.criteria: Create a full-screen image readable at arm's length.

checkpoints.title: Ship it in a pack
checkpoints.practice:
Put your images into a pack and send it to an Atlas.

Then hand it to somebody who has not seen it.

Watch which images they pause on and which they scroll past.
checkpoints.criteria: Deploy artwork to another person's device and observe their response.

skills.objective: Map branching stories or light shows, deploy complete packs, and configure startup behavior.

checkpoints.title: The map
checkpoints.practice: Plan either a branching story with at least eight scenes and three endings, or an instructor-approved light show. Draw every scene and transition before building. Trace each route to confirm it reaches an intended ending.
checkpoints.criteria: Draw a complete map with valid routes from start to endings.

checkpoints.title: Built and shipped
checkpoints.practice: Build the complete pack from your map and test every route. Invite a new user to find two endings, or watch the complete show, while you observe without prompting. Revise any confusing transition.
checkpoints.criteria: Let a new user reach two endings or complete the show unaided.

checkpoints.title: Set the boot
checkpoints.practice: Community has a set boot mode option: an Atlas can wake up straight into a pack.
checkpoints.criteria: Set the pack to launch at boot and restore the previous setting.

skills.title: Save your work properly
skills.objective: Organize current files, preserve working versions, record changes, and recover lost work.

checkpoints.title: Set up the folder
checkpoints.practice:
Your folder on the project drive.

1. One folder per project, not one folder for everything.
2. A notes file in each.
3. A copy of the current working version, named properly.
4. A second copy somewhere else. The drive and a memory stick, or the drive and your own machine.
checkpoints.criteria: Make the current version identifiable within five seconds.

checkpoints.title: Break it and go back
checkpoints.practice:
Deliberately.

1. Save a working version.
2. Then wreck the working copy. Really wreck it.
3. Then restore from your saved version and carry on.
4. Everybody should do this once on purpose so the first time is not a real emergency.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate recovery from a deliberate destructive edit in under two minutes.

checkpoints.title: Keep the notes
checkpoints.practice:
Work a real project across at least three sessions.

Every save gets a line in notes: date, what changed, works or does not.

No exceptions, including the sessions where nothing worked.
checkpoints.criteria: Keep honest change notes across three sessions, including a failure.

checkpoints.title: Recover something real
checkpoints.practice:
Sooner or later something will genuinely go wrong. A crash, a bad edit, a file that will not open.

When it does, recover it from your own versions and explain to your instructor how long it took.
checkpoints.criteria: Recover a real loss independently using your version system.

skills.title: The community game
skills.objective: Define simple game rules, test them on paper, and ship a playable Community project.

checkpoints.title: The four lines
checkpoints.practice:
Write your goal, your rule, your pressure and your end.

Four lines, on one card.

If any of them takes more than a line, the game is too big for this badge.
checkpoints.criteria: Explain the game through the required four concise lines.

checkpoints.title: Play it on paper
checkpoints.practice:
Before you build it, play it.

Pencil, paper, dice if you need them. Play three full games.

Write down what was boring, what was unfair, and what you kept wanting to do that the rules did not allow.
checkpoints.criteria: Revise at least one rule after paper playtesting.

checkpoints.title: Build it and ship it
checkpoints.practice:
Now build it in Maker and send it to an Atlas.

It has to start, play, and end, on the device, without you standing there.

Written for the small screen, and with art that reads. You have badges for both.
checkpoints.criteria: Publish a clearly named game that works from beginning to end.

checkpoints.practice:
The real test of a game.

Hand it to somebody who has never seen it. Say nothing.

The pass is not that they finish it. The pass is that they start it again.
checkpoints.criteria: Have an unrelated player voluntarily play twice consecutively.

skills.title: Playtest

checkpoints.title: Sit on your hands
checkpoints.practice:
One person, your work, ten minutes, and you say nothing after the first sentence.

Write down everything.

This will be genuinely hard. Everybody wants to help. That is why it is a checkpoint.
checkpoints.criteria: Observe silently and record at least ten findings.

checkpoints.title: Three testers, one pattern
checkpoints.practice:
Do it three times with three different people.

Then look at your three sets of notes and find what all three did.

That thing is real. Anything only one person did might just be that person.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify a problem encountered by all three testers.

checkpoints.title: Fix the pattern, not the complaint
checkpoints.practice:
Take the thing all three hit.

Work out what the actual problem is, which is usually not what any of them suggested.

Fix it, and write down what you changed and why.
checkpoints.criteria: Fix the underlying issue and explain the design decision.

checkpoints.title: Test it again
checkpoints.practice:
Three new people. Same silence, same notes.

Did the problem go away? Did you make a new one?

checkpoints.title: One line at a time
checkpoints.practice: Start with a known working example. Change one line, predict its effect, run it, and explain the result. Repeat with three distinct changes, keeping a recoverable working version.
checkpoints.criteria: Explain three individual changes made to a working recipe.

checkpoints.title: The deliberate break
checkpoints.practice: Make a copy of the working program and introduce one small, reversible error. Read the diagnostic message, locate the affected line, explain the cause, and repair it. Run the original behavior again to verify the fix.
checkpoints.criteria: Introduce, interpret, and repair a deliberate coding error.

checkpoints.title: Something moves
checkpoints.practice: Take the shapes recipe and make something move under controller input.
checkpoints.criteria: Make an on-screen shape respond to controls.

skills.title: Sprites and movement
skills.objective: Implement responsive movement, separate update and draw logic, and manage multiple sprites.

checkpoints.title: Move one thing
checkpoints.practice:
Start from a working recipe.

1. Get one sprite on screen.
2. Make it move with the controller.
3. Put its speed in a variable and change the variable to change the feel.
4. Stop it leaving the screen.
checkpoints.criteria: Tune a movement property through a single numeric change.

checkpoints.title: Split update from draw
checkpoints.practice:
Look at your code and separate it properly.

Everything that decides goes in one place. Everything that draws goes in another.

Then prove it: comment out the draw and the game still runs, silently, with everything still moving. Print a position to check.
checkpoints.criteria: Separate state updates from drawing and demonstrate updates without rendering.

checkpoints.title: Many things at once
checkpoints.practice:
One moving thing is a demo. Several is a game.

1. Get at least five sprites moving at once.
2. Give them different speeds and directions.
3. Handle them as a group rather than writing the same code five times.
checkpoints.criteria: Move at least five independent objects with easy extension to a sixth.

checkpoints.title: Make it feel good
checkpoints.practice:
The part that is design, not code.

1. Add acceleration so it does not start and stop instantly.
2. Or add a tiny delay, or a slight overshoot.
3. Change one thing at a time and hand the controls to somebody after each change.
4. Feel is made of very small numbers and there is no formula. There is only trying it and asking somebody.
checkpoints.criteria: Improve motion so an independent user notices better feel.

skills.title: Collision and rules
skills.objective: Add reliable collisions, visible consequences, game states, and progressive challenge.

checkpoints.title: Two things touch
checkpoints.practice:
Get two sprites and detect when they overlap.

Draw the boxes on screen temporarily so you can see what you are actually testing.

Then check the edges: exactly touching, one pixel apart, one pixel overlapping.
checkpoints.criteria: Verify collision detection at object edges as well as centers.

checkpoints.title: Something happens
checkpoints.practice:
On contact, do something that matters.

1. A score that goes up and is visible.
2. A life that goes down and is visible.
3. Something that disappears, or bounces, or changes.
checkpoints.criteria: Make the consequence of contact immediately visible.

checkpoints.title: States that work
checkpoints.practice:
Title, playing, game over, and back to playing.

1. One state variable.
2. A title screen that says what to press.
3. A game over that shows the score.
4. A way back to playing that fully resets everything.
5. Fully resets is the hard part. Score, lives, positions, timers, everything.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete five play, loss, and restart cycles without stale state.

checkpoints.title: Make it get harder
checkpoints.practice:
A game with no escalation is a demo.

Add one thing that ramps: speed, quantity, a timer running down, a gap closing.

Tune it so a first time player lasts somewhere between thirty seconds and two minutes.
checkpoints.criteria: Create difficulty that leads a new player to seek another attempt.

skills.title: Sound and music
skills.objective: Design coherent effects and looping music while retaining playable visual feedback.

checkpoints.title: One good bleep
checkpoints.practice:
Make one feedback sound for one action, and get it right.

1. Short enough that it never overlaps itself.
2. Triggered on the event, not every frame.
3. Pitch varied slightly each time.
4. Then play it a hundred times in a row and see whether you still like it.
checkpoints.criteria: Create an effect tolerable over one hundred repetitions.

checkpoints.title: A sound set
checkpoints.practice:
Four or five sounds that belong together.

Action, success, failure, and something ambient.

They should sound like they came from the same machine.
checkpoints.criteria: Make a coherent set whose individual sounds remain distinct.

checkpoints.title: Music that loops
checkpoints.practice:
A short piece that loops without a seam.

Play it for five minutes. Then leave it playing while you do something else for another five.

If you notice the join, it is not finished.
checkpoints.criteria: Loop music for ten minutes without an audible seam.

checkpoints.title: Play it muted
checkpoints.practice:
Turn all the sound off and play your game.

Everything important should still be clear.

Then turn it back on and notice how much better it feels.
checkpoints.criteria: Keep the game playable when muted and better with sound enabled.

checkpoints.practice: Write the game on an index card. What the player does, how it gets harder, how it ends.
checkpoints.criteria: Fit the complete game scope onto one planning card.

checkpoints.practice: Use your planning card as a test checklist. Play from the start through each planned interaction, increasing difficulty, and the ending. Record defects, fix them, and repeat the complete run before exporting.

checkpoints.title: On the slate
checkpoints.practice: Export, carry it over, load it on the Locke.
checkpoints.criteria: Have another person play the exported cartridge on the television.

checkpoints.title: A map from data
checkpoints.practice:
Build a level as a grid of numbers, separate from your code.

Draw it on paper first, then type it in.

Then change the paper, change the data, and see the level change without touching any logic.
checkpoints.criteria: Redesign the level through data changes without code changes.

checkpoints.title: Collide with the map
checkpoints.practice:
The player stops at walls, stands on floors, and cannot leave the map.

Work it out from the tile the player is in, not by checking every wall in the level.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate reliable movement and collisions at full speed.

checkpoints.title: A camera that does not annoy
checkpoints.practice:
Make the world bigger than the screen and follow the player.

1. Loose following, not locked.
2. Clamped at the map edges.
3. A little look ahead in the direction of travel.
4. Then hand it to somebody and watch their head. If they lean, the camera is wrong.
checkpoints.criteria: Let another person play comfortably with the camera for two minutes.

checkpoints.title: Design a real level
checkpoints.practice:
One level that teaches, tests and combines.

1. Introduce one idea in a place where failing costs nothing.
2. Then use it where failing costs something.
3. Then combine it with something they already know.
4. No text tutorial. The level teaches, or it does not.
checkpoints.criteria: Observe a new player learning the mechanic from level design alone.

checkpoints.title: Ask properly
checkpoints.practice:
Take a real problem in one of your own projects.

Write the prompt before you type it: what the project is, what the code does, what you tried, what happened, and what you want.

Then compare the answer against a lazy version of the same question.
checkpoints.criteria: Compare two answers and explain how prompt changes affected them.

checkpoints.title: Explain before write
checkpoints.practice:
Find something in a codebase you do not understand.

1. Paste it and ask Eddy to explain it.
2. Read the explanation and decide whether you believe it.
3. Then check it against the actual behaviour by changing something and seeing what happens.
checkpoints.criteria: Find an incorrect model explanation through testing.

checkpoints.title: Build something with it
checkpoints.practice:
A real feature in a real project of yours.

1. Work in small steps. Ask, test, keep or discard.
2. Version your work as you go. Save Your Work Properly exists for exactly this.
3. Keep a known good copy before every significant change.
4. Reject things. Discarding a suggestion is the skill, not accepting one.
checkpoints.criteria: Integrate a working feature and explain every line.

checkpoints.title: Do it without
checkpoints.practice:
The one that proves the badge.

Take a similar sized problem and solve it with Eddy switched off.

It will take longer. That is fine and it is the point.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate programming the feature's essential work without the model.

skills.title: Read what eddy wrote
skills.objective: Review generated and human code, design edge tests, and verify confident technical claims.

checkpoints.title: Find the planted bugs
checkpoints.practice:
We give you five pieces of code, each with one fault. Some are ours, some are Eddy's.

Find them all. You may run them, and you should.
checkpoints.criteria: Find at least four planted bugs and specify triggering inputs.

checkpoints.title: Test the edges
checkpoints.practice:
Take a working function, yours or Eddy's.

Write down every edge case you can think of before testing any of them. Aim for eight.

Then test all of them.
checkpoints.criteria: Use systematic edge cases to find an overlooked behavior.

checkpoints.title: Catch a confident lie
checkpoints.practice:
Deliberately push Eddy into territory where it will invent something.

Ask about an obscure part of a library, or a function with a plausible name.

Then verify against real documentation.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate a confidently false model claim and how it was disproved.

checkpoints.title: Review a person
checkpoints.practice:
Somebody else's real code, with their permission.

1. Say what it is supposed to do, in your words, and check with them.
2. Test it, do not just read it.
3. Report what you found: what is wrong, what input shows it, why it matters.
4. No style opinions unless they ask.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify a genuine issue in another person's code constructively.

skills.title: Ship to the shelf

checkpoints.title: Finish it
checkpoints.practice:
Take something to actually done.

1. Title screen with name, author and version.
2. Every state reachable and every state escapable.
3. No placeholder art, no debug text, no dead menu items.
4. It runs on the real hardware it is for, not just in preview.
5. Done is a checklist, not a feeling.
checkpoints.criteria: Deliver work a stranger can use without guidance.

checkpoints.title: Write the readme
checkpoints.practice:
One page.

1. What it is, in one sentence.
2. How to play, in five lines.
3. What is new in this version.
4. Known problems, honestly listed.
5. How to tell you about a bug.
6. The known problems section is the one that shows you are serious. Everybody has them. Listing them is what makes people trust the rest.
checkpoints.criteria: Write instructions sufficient for a new user to play correctly.

checkpoints.title: Ship it and watch
checkpoints.practice:
Onto the shelf.

Then run a proper playtest round with strangers, using everything the Playtest badge taught you.

Say nothing. Write everything down.
checkpoints.criteria: Observe at least five independent players and record their behavior.

checkpoints.title: Ship it again
checkpoints.practice:
The checkpoint that makes this a capstone.

1. Fix what the testers actually hit, not what you wish they had hit.
2. Bump the version number.
3. Update the readme, including what changed.
4. Put it back on the shelf.
checkpoints.criteria: Publish a second version based on feedback with updated documentation.

checkpoints.title: Hand it over
checkpoints.practice:
The last one, and the one nobody expects.

Write up how somebody else could pick your project up and continue it.

Where the files are, how to build it, what is half finished, what you would do next.
checkpoints.criteria: Package the project so another person could maintain it.

skills.title: Paper and stomp
skills.objective: Build and improve stomp-launched paper rockets through measured, controlled comparisons.

checkpoints.title: Build one that flies
checkpoints.practice:
Body, sealed nose, fins, and it slides off the tube freely.

Then fly it three times and measure how far it went each time.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete three straight flights with the rocket still reusable.

checkpoints.title: Change one thing
checkpoints.practice:
Now the actual skill.

1. Fly your rocket three times and take the average distance. That is your baseline.
2. Change exactly one thing. Fin size, fin count, body length, nose shape, or a little weight in the nose.
3. Fly three more and average again.
4. Write both numbers down.
5. Three flights per version, because one flight tells you almost nothing. Wind, your jump and luck are all bigger than most of the changes you will make.
checkpoints.criteria: Compare two three-flight averages after changing one variable.

checkpoints.title: Find what actually matters
checkpoints.practice:
Test four different changes, properly, three flights each.

Then rank them: which change made the biggest difference?

Most people are surprised. Nose weight usually beats everything and nobody expects it.
checkpoints.criteria: Rank four tested changes using recorded measurements.

checkpoints.title: Build the best one
checkpoints.practice:
Take everything you learned and build one final rocket.

Then fly it against somebody else's in a straight comparison, same board, same session.
checkpoints.criteria: Beat the original rocket's performance and explain the successful changes.

skills.title: Why it flies straight
skills.objective: Locate stability reference points, compare swing tests, and assess other rockets.

checkpoints.title: Find both points
checkpoints.practice:
On a real rocket, loaded the way it will fly.

1. Balance it to find CG. Mark it with tape.
2. Estimate CP: cut the rocket's side profile out of card and balance that. The balance point of the flat shape is a good enough CP.
3. Mark both and measure the gap in body diameters.
checkpoints.criteria: Mark both reference points, measure their separation, and judge stability.

checkpoints.title: The swing test
checkpoints.practice:
The proof, and it is genuinely satisfying.

1. Tie a string around the rocket at the CG so it hangs level.
2. Take it outside, well clear of everybody.
3. Swing it round your head in a big circle.
4. A stable rocket points where it is going. An unstable one tumbles.
5. Two metres of clear space in every direction, minimum, and check behind you before you start.
checkpoints.criteria: Compare the behavior of stable and unstable rockets in swing tests.

checkpoints.title: Fix an unstable one
checkpoints.practice:
We will hand you a bird that does not pass.

Diagnose it, choose a fix, apply it, and prove it with the swing test.

Then say what your fix cost you.
checkpoints.criteria: Make an unstable rocket pass and explain the tradeoff.

checkpoints.title: Check somebody else's bird
checkpoints.practice:
Somebody else's rocket, before it flies.

Find both points, measure the margin, give them a verdict and a reason.

Be right. This is a real job on launch day and somebody's rocket depends on it.
checkpoints.criteria: Give another builder an assessment consistent with staff findings.

checkpoints.title: Build and check
checkpoints.practice:
A bottle rocket with fins and a nose.

1. Approved bottle, undamaged, inspected by you.
2. Fins attached so they do not peel off when wet. Tape that survives water, or fins that clip on.
3. A nose cone, and nose weight if it needs it.
4. Stability checked with the swing test, loaded with water.
5. Loaded with water is the important bit. A bottle rocket's CG moves a long way when you fill it.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a loaded rocket that passes stability and handling checks.

checkpoints.title: Run the range
checkpoints.practice:
The procedure, out loud, every flight.

1. Rocket on the launcher, everybody behind the line.
2. Call the range hot.
3. Pump, calling the pressure out loud as it climbs.
4. Stop at the limit and say the number.
5. Count down, release.
6. Range stays hot until the rocket is down and still.
checkpoints.criteria: Follow the full range procedure and respect its limit without reminders.

checkpoints.title: Find the best fill
checkpoints.practice:
The experiment this rocket was born for.

1. Same bottle, same pressure, three flights each.
2. Try a quarter full, a third, half, and two thirds.
3. Measure how high or how far each one goes.
4. Average, compare, and pick a winner.
checkpoints.criteria: Compare four average results and identify the best tested fill.

checkpoints.criteria: Coach a learner who flies safely and can repeat the rules.

skills.title: Recovery systems
skills.objective: Construct, test, pack, and prepare parachute recovery systems for others.

checkpoints.title: Make a chute
checkpoints.practice:
From the kit.

1. Cut the canopy accurately. Uneven canopies fly sideways.
2. Reinforce every shroud line attachment point. That is where they always fail.
3. Shroud lines all the same length. Measure, do not eyeball.
4. Attach to the rocket with something that can swivel, or the lines will twist and collapse it.
checkpoints.criteria: Make an even canopy with equal lines and reinforced attachments.

checkpoints.title: Drop test it
checkpoints.practice:
Outside the rocket, from a height, with a weight on it that matches the bird.

1. Five drops, minimum.
2. It has to open every time.
3. Time the descent and see whether it is sensible for your field.
4. The stairwell works, and so does a first floor window with permission and a spotter.
checkpoints.criteria: Achieve five clean drop openings and record descent time.

checkpoints.title: Pack it properly
checkpoints.practice:
Into the rocket, with wadding, the way it will fly.

1. Wadding first, enough of it.
2. Chute folded loose, lines gathered but not bound.
3. Nose seated firm but removable by hand.
4. Then deploy it by hand five times without repacking from scratch each time.
checkpoints.criteria: Achieve five clean deployments from the packed rocket.

checkpoints.title: Pack for somebody else
checkpoints.practice:
Their bird, their flight, your packing.

Talk them through what you are doing and why, so they can do their own next time.

Then watch it fly and see whether it came out.
checkpoints.criteria: Prepare another person's recovery system for a successful flight.

skills.title: The payload
skills.objective: Design and test protected payloads, reassess loaded stability, and gather flight observations.

checkpoints.title: The egg
checkpoints.practice:
One raw egg, up and back, unbroken.

1. Design a bay and a cushion.
2. Test on the ground first: drop it from a metre onto a hard floor inside the bay.
3. Fix what breaks. Test again.
4. Then fly it.
checkpoints.criteria: Recover an intact egg after ground testing and a real flight.

checkpoints.title: Rebalance, loaded
checkpoints.practice:
With the payload in, every time.

1. Find the CG loaded.
2. Compare to the CP.
3. Adjust with nose weight if you need to.
4. Swing test it loaded.
checkpoints.criteria: Measure the loaded center-of-gravity change and pass the stability test.

checkpoints.title: Carry a camera
checkpoints.practice:
A camera up and back, with footage.

1. Mounted so it cannot move.
2. Pointing at something worth seeing, and think about which way.
3. Started before the bird goes on the pad, because you will not be going back to it.
4. Balance rechecked.
checkpoints.criteria: Obtain flight footage with the camera intact afterwards.

checkpoints.title: Fly something of your own choosing
checkpoints.practice:
Your payload, your reason.

It has to be something you can say something about afterwards. A sensor, a message, an experiment, a small thing that belongs to somebody.

Then report on it: what you sent, what happened, what you learned.
checkpoints.criteria: Fly a chosen payload and record a meaningful observation.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.

skills.title: Measure the sky
skills.objective: Predict altitude, collect flight data, explain discrepancies, and compare repeated flights.

checkpoints.title: Predict first
checkpoints.practice:
Before a flight, on paper:

1. Weigh the bird, loaded, motor in.
2. Note the motor.
3. Run the simulation, or do the arithmetic.
4. Write down your predicted altitude and sign it.
5. Signed and dated before the flight. That is what makes it a prediction rather than a memory.
checkpoints.criteria: Write and date an altitude prediction before launch.

checkpoints.title: Fly it and read it
checkpoints.practice:
Altimeter mounted, vented, armed, checked.

Fly, recover, and read the number before anything else happens.

Write it in the flight data log next to your prediction.
checkpoints.criteria: Record actual altitude beside the prediction.

checkpoints.title: Explain the gap
checkpoints.practice:
They will not match. They never do.

Work out why, and test your explanation on the next flight by changing one thing.

1. Sand and polish the bird for drag.
2. Check the fins are true.
3. Reweigh and rerun the prediction.
4. Fly again on the same motor.
checkpoints.criteria: Improve a second prediction and explain the changed assumptions.

checkpoints.title: Three flights, one bird
checkpoints.practice:
Same bird, same motor, three flights across the day.

Record all three altitudes and the wind conditions each time.

Then say how repeatable your rocket actually is.
checkpoints.criteria: Log three flights with conditions and describe the observed spread.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Use of altimeters and the flight-data log.

skills.title: Design your own bird
skills.objective: Specify, model, print, test, fly, and publish an original rocket design.

checkpoints.title: The mission and the maths
checkpoints.practice:
One sheet, before any modelling.

1. The mission, in one sentence.
2. The motor, and why that one.
3. Body diameter, length, fin size, all with reasons.
4. Predicted CG, predicted CP, and the margin in calibres.
5. A simulated altitude.
checkpoints.criteria: Justify the design figures and provide at least one-caliber stability margin.

checkpoints.title: Design and print it
checkpoints.practice:
In Onshape, as components, designed for the machine.

Print the set. Test fit every joint before you glue anything.

Expect a version two on at least one part. Everybody has one.
checkpoints.criteria: Print a complete, support-free set with strong fins and sound dry fits.

checkpoints.title: Prove it on the ground
checkpoints.practice:
Before it goes near a field.

1. Build it, loaded, and weigh it.
2. Rerun the simulation with the real mass.
3. Find the real CG loaded and mark it.
4. Swing test it loaded.
5. Full flight check card.
6. Recovery drop tested five out of five.
checkpoints.criteria: Pass all ground checks and prepare a labeled flight-ready rocket.

checkpoints.title: Fly it twice
checkpoints.practice:
Two flights, with an altimeter, with a prediction each time.

1. First flight: fly it, recover it, read it, inspect it.
2. Between flights: look at everything. Fins, motor mount, nose fit, any cracks.
3. Second flight: with whatever you learned applied and a new prediction.
4. The first flight is data. Treat it that way and the second one is much better.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete two predicted and measured flights while retaining a flyable rocket.

checkpoints.title: Put it in the library
checkpoints.practice:
So somebody else can fly it.

1. Fix what the flights taught you.
2. Name the files clearly and say which way each part prints.
3. Write the build note: parts, print settings, glue points, motor, expected altitude, nose weight required.
4. Include the stability numbers so the next person can check them.
checkpoints.criteria: Have another person print and fly the documented design independently.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: Ground checks, range rules, and staff assessment apply to flight activities.

skills.title: The rover brain
skills.objective: Assemble and verify the Pioneer controller, power rails, and breadboard connections.

checkpoints.title: Seat and power
checkpoints.practice: Disconnect power and check the exact controller pinout. Seat the board squarely without bending pins, then have the instructor inspect supply polarity and connections before first power-up.
checkpoints.criteria: Seat and power the controller correctly without bent connections.

checkpoints.title: Read your own board
checkpoints.practice: Trace the complete power route from the supply through the rails to the controller. Label each connection on a drawing and compare it with the board documentation. Check for split rails rather than assuming they are continuous.
checkpoints.criteria: Trace and name the complete power path on the board.

checkpoints.title: The pull test
checkpoints.practice: Not a tug of war. Tip the board upside down and shake gently.
checkpoints.criteria: Pass the connection retention test without loose wires.

skills.preparation: Confirm the exact hardware, pinout, voltage, current limits, and manufacturer instructions. Disconnect power before assembly. An instructor checks wiring and battery arrangements before first power-up.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Use of the rover bench, using the learner's own Atlas.

skills.title: Legs and muscle
skills.objective: Connect the motor driver, test both directions, and make the rover move predictably.

checkpoints.title: Power where power belongs
checkpoints.practice: Draw separate paths for the controller supply and motor supply using the approved driver documentation. Identify the required ground connections and explain why motor current must not pass through a controller signal pin.
checkpoints.criteria: Explain the separate motor and controller power paths.

checkpoints.title: The spin test
checkpoints.practice: With the wheels OFF the ground on the stand, power up and run the workshop test that twitches each motor.
checkpoints.criteria: Run both motors in both directions without abnormal heating.

checkpoints.title: Roll it
checkpoints.practice: Floor, flat run, gentle test.
checkpoints.criteria: Make forward commands move forward and identify any required wiring correction.

skills.title: Take the wheel
skills.objective: Pair an Atlas with its rover and practice controlled driving and deliveries.

checkpoints.title: Find and bind
checkpoints.practice: Identify your rover by its configured name. Connect the controller, test a low-speed command in a clear area, disconnect, and reconnect. Confirm the rover stops safely when control is lost.
checkpoints.criteria: Find, connect, disconnect, and reconnect to the correct named rover.

checkpoints.title: The lane
checkpoints.practice: Drive the workshop lane: out, around the cone, and home.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete a contact-free lap using forward, turning, and spinning.

checkpoints.title: The delivery
checkpoints.practice: A small load goes on the rover deck. Drive it across the room and deliver it to a person without them having to catch anything.
checkpoints.criteria: Deliver a load and stop gently for unloading.

skills.preparation: Confirm the exact hardware, pinout, voltage, current limits, and manufacturer instructions. Disconnect power before assembly. An instructor checks wiring and battery arrangements before first power-up.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Use of the workshop driving lane with the Atlas-controlled rover.

skills.title: Trim and tune
skills.objective: Measure drift, tune steering and traction, and improve driving through timed comparisons.

checkpoints.title: Measure the drift
checkpoints.practice:
Three metres, straight, full forward, no steering input at all.

1. Mark the start and the aim point.
2. Drive it and measure the offset at the end.
3. Do it three times and average.
4. Then do the same in reverse.
checkpoints.criteria: Record drift in both directions over three meters.

checkpoints.title: Trim it out
checkpoints.practice:
Now fix it in the machine.

1. Adjust the motor trim.
2. Run the same three metre test.
3. One change per run. Write each one down.
4. Keep going until the drift is under about ten centimetres in three metres.
checkpoints.criteria: Reduce drift below ten centimeters over three meters using recorded adjustments.

checkpoints.title: Tyres and weight
checkpoints.practice:
Change the grip and see what it costs.

1. Time a straight sprint and a spin on the spot, as you are.
2. Add tyres or grip. Time both again.
3. Move the pack forward and back. Time both again.
4. Find the combination that is best for the derby, not best at one thing.
checkpoints.criteria: Compare tire and weight setups using times and explained compromises.

checkpoints.title: Drive a clean lap
checkpoints.practice:
The workshop lane, timed, with your tuned rover.

Not the fastest lap. A clean one: no walls, no corrections mid straight, gentle stops.

Then a faster one that is still clean.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete two contact-free laps with the second faster.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.

skills.title: Derby clearance
skills.objective: Plan and drive the full derby course, handling obstacles consistently before timed runs.

checkpoints.title: Walk it and plan it
checkpoints.practice:
On foot, before you drive.

1. Walk the whole course.
2. Decide your line at every obstacle.
3. Decide where you will go fast and where you will go slow.
4. Say it out loud to somebody before you start.
checkpoints.criteria: Explain a route that includes deliberate slow sections.

checkpoints.title: Clear every obstacle
checkpoints.practice:
One at a time, no clock.

Each obstacle, cleanly, three times in a row before you move on to the next.

Three in a row, because once is luck.
checkpoints.criteria: Clear each obstacle three consecutive times.

checkpoints.title: A clean run
checkpoints.practice:
The whole course, start to finish box, no clock.

Clean means no cones, no walls, no rescues, and a controlled stop in the box.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete one full course without contact or intervention.

checkpoints.title: A timed run
checkpoints.practice:
Now with the clock.

Post a time on a clean run. Then beat it.

The time does not have to be fast. It has to be yours and it has to be clean.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete two clean timed runs and improve the second time.

skills.preparation: Confirm the exact hardware, pinout, voltage, current limits, and manufacturer instructions. Disconnect power before assembly. An instructor checks wiring and battery arrangements before first power-up.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Entry to Pioneer Derby and use of the full obstacle course.

skills.title: Design your chassis
skills.objective: Specify and print a custom chassis, validate mounts, and compare it against the kit rover.

checkpoints.title: Measure and decide
checkpoints.practice:
One sheet before any modelling.

1. Every component measured by you: motors, mounting pattern, pack, board, wheels.
2. Your chosen wheelbase, track and clearance, each with a reason.
3. Where the pack sits and why.
4. What you are optimising for: derby time, sumo, load carrying, or looks. Pick one and say it.
checkpoints.criteria: Justify dimensions against one clearly stated design priority.

checkpoints.title: Test print the mounts
checkpoints.practice:
Before the chassis.

1. Just the motor mount, on its own.
2. Fit a real motor.
3. Load it. Push, twist, and drop it from a metre.
4. Fix and repeat until it survives.
checkpoints.criteria: Print a motor mount that holds firmly and survives the specified test.

checkpoints.title: Build it and drive it
checkpoints.practice:
Print the chassis, move everything across, and drive it.

Then run the same tuning tests: drift, sprint, spin, and a lap.

Compare against the kit chassis numbers you already have.
checkpoints.criteria: Measure driving differences and compare them with the design intent.

checkpoints.title: Survive the course
checkpoints.practice:
The derby course, three full runs, including the ramp and the gap.

Then inspect it. Every mount, every joint, every wheel.

Fix what moved and note what you would change in version two.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete three course runs without breakage and identify developing looseness.

skills.preparation: Confirm the exact hardware, pinout, voltage, current limits, and manufacturer instructions. Disconnect power before assembly. An instructor checks wiring and battery arrangements before first power-up.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Custom-chassis derby entry and publication in the rover library.

skills.title: Lights and sound
skills.objective: Budget and secure rover lighting and sound, communicate actions, and test night driving.

checkpoints.title: Budget it first
checkpoints.practice:
Before you fit anything.

1. Count the LEDs you want.
2. Multiply by sixty milliamps.
3. Find out what your pack delivers and what the motors take when they start.
4. Decide how many LEDs and at what brightness.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a realistic power budget before fitting accessories.

checkpoints.title: Fit them so they stay on
checkpoints.practice:
Printed housings, dressed wiring, strain relief.

Then the test: three runs of the derby course, including the ramp and the gap.
checkpoints.criteria: Keep all accessories secure and working over three runs.

checkpoints.title: Make them mean something
checkpoints.practice:
At least three behaviours:

1. Headlights that respond to driving forward.
2. A reverse indication.
3. Something that shows a state: connected, low battery, or which mode it is in.
4. A person watching should be able to tell what the rover is doing without seeing your hands.
checkpoints.criteria: Make rover actions understandable from lighting across the room.

checkpoints.title: Drive it in the dark
checkpoints.practice:
Lights off in the room, course lit only by your rover.

Drive a clean lap.

Then find out what you cannot see and add light there.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete a clean dark lap and improve a visibility problem.

skills.preparation: Confirm the exact hardware, pinout, voltage, current limits, and manufacturer instructions. Disconnect power before assembly. An instructor checks wiring and battery arrangements before first power-up.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Rover modification stock and night use of the driving lane.

skills.title: Sensors and autonomy
skills.objective: Characterize sensors and implement obstacle stopping, line following, and safe autonomous behavior.

checkpoints.title: One sensor, characterised
checkpoints.practice:
Pick one and find out what it really does.

1. Measure known distances and compare with what it reports.
2. Find the closest and furthest it works.
3. Find three things it gets wrong: a soft surface, an angled surface, a narrow object.
4. Write all of it down.
checkpoints.criteria: Document one sensor's operating range and failure conditions.

checkpoints.title: Stop before the wall
checkpoints.practice:
The first autonomous behaviour.

1. Wheels up on the stand first. Watch it decide.
2. Then on the floor, slowly.
3. It drives forward and stops before the wall. Every time, from three different starting distances.
4. Then take the wall away and check it stops anyway rather than driving forever.
checkpoints.criteria: Stop reliably from three distances and handle absent-wall conditions safely.

checkpoints.title: Follow a line
checkpoints.practice:
Calibrate, then follow.

1. Calibrate on the actual surface, in the actual light.
2. Follow a straight line.
3. Then a curve.
4. Then handle losing the line: stop, or search, but do something deliberate.
checkpoints.criteria: Follow a curved line and respond sensibly when it is lost.

checkpoints.title: Autonomous run, hands off
checkpoints.practice:
A full course, autonomously, with your hands behind your back.

1. Start it and step away.
2. No touching, no input, no help.
3. It finishes, or it stops safely.
4. An edge sensor that stops it going off the table counts as finishing well.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete an autonomous run or stop correctly without human control.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: The autonomy sensor set and entry to autonomous events.

skills.title: The work rover
skills.objective: Prototype and build a powered rover mechanism that performs a useful task.

checkpoints.title: Card prototype
checkpoints.practice:
The mechanism, in card, before anything is printed.

1. Cut the arms and links from card.
2. Pin the pivots.
3. Move it through its full range by hand.
4. Find where it binds, where it cannot reach, and where it goes over centre.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate full motion in card and correct a geometry problem early.

checkpoints.title: Build the mechanism
checkpoints.practice:
Print it, mount it, drive it with a servo.

1. Rigid servo mount.
2. Pivots with clearance, from your fit test.
3. End stops so it cannot drive itself into a limit and stall.
4. Separate power feed for the servo.
checkpoints.criteria: Run the mechanism through its range without stalling or supply resets.

checkpoints.title: Do the job
checkpoints.practice:
A real task, completed, on the floor.

1. Define the task before you start: what, from where, to where, how many.
2. Drive it and do the job.
3. Time it.
4. Then do it three times in a row to prove it was not luck.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete the task three consecutive times with recorded timings.

checkpoints.title: Do it for somebody
checkpoints.practice:
A real job somebody in the workshop actually wants doing.

Fetching parts down the bench, delivering something across the room, clearing scrap off the mat.

Do it for a week.
checkpoints.criteria: Perform a real task requested by another person.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Mechanisms, servos, gears, and grippers, plus task-event entry.

skills.title: The battle bot
skills.objective: Build an arena-compliant pushing rover, test its wedge, repair between matches, and compete fairly.

checkpoints.title: Build to the rules
checkpoints.practice:
Read the rules card and build to it.

1. Weigh it on the scale.
2. Check every fastener.
3. Nothing sharp, nothing loose, nothing that spins.
4. Get it inspected before you assume it will pass.
checkpoints.criteria: Pass the dimensional, weight, and rules inspection immediately.

checkpoints.title: The wedge works
checkpoints.practice:
Test it against a stationary rover before any match.

1. Drive at it square and get under.
2. Push it three metres in a straight line.
3. Then try from an angle and see what happens.
checkpoints.criteria: Consistently engage and push a stationary rover using the wedge.

checkpoints.title: Fight and fix
checkpoints.practice:
Three matches, and repairs between them.

Things will break. The badge is not about winning, it is about what you do in the four minutes between rounds.

Bring spares. Everybody who does well brings spares.
checkpoints.criteria: Reach the third match with a working machine after your own repair.

checkpoints.title: Shake hands
checkpoints.practice:
The one that actually matters.

Win or lose, afterwards: talk to the other builder about their machine, and tell them one thing you thought was good about it.

Then explain to your instructor one thing you are stealing for version two.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate sportsmanship and identify an improvement learned from an opponent.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Arena participation under the combat-class rules.

skills.title: The airship
skills.objective: Design a lightweight Pioneer airship, manage buoyancy, and demonstrate controlled indoor flight.

checkpoints.title: The mass budget
checkpoints.practice:
Before anything is built.

1. Every component weighed individually, on the small scale, and written down.
2. A total for the whole machine.
3. Envelope volume needed to lift that, at roughly one gram per litre.
4. Then a second column: where you can save grams, and how many.
checkpoints.criteria: Close the mass budget with margin and identify at least ten grams of savings.

checkpoints.title: Build it light
checkpoints.practice:
The gondola, the mounts, and everything that hangs under the envelope.

1. Printed parts thinned and hollowed to the edge of what will survive.
2. Wires cut to length, no spare loops.
3. No fastener heavier than it has to be.
4. Weigh the finished thing and compare with your budget.
checkpoints.criteria: Build within ten percent of the predicted mass.

checkpoints.title: Trim to neutral
checkpoints.practice:
With staff, and with the room settled.

1. Inflate, with us.
2. Add small weights until it neither rises nor sinks.
3. Move the weights until it hangs level.
4. Let it sit for five minutes and check again, because helium and temperature both change things.
checkpoints.criteria: Hold level and stationary without power for one minute.

checkpoints.title: Fly it
checkpoints.practice:
Your Atlas, your airship, a big room with the fans off.

1. Forward, and stop before the wall. This will take several attempts.
2. A turn, controlled.
3. A full circuit of the room without touching anything.
4. Then land it gently in a marked area.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete a circuit and controlled landing without contact.

checkpoints.title: Hand over the controls
checkpoints.practice:
Teach somebody else to fly it.

Everything about coasting, drift, and giving the input early.

Hands off. They fly it.
checkpoints.criteria: Teach another person to complete a controlled straight run and stop.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.

skills.title: The 5v strip
skills.objective: Identify polarity, cut and mount plain 5 V LED strips, and integrate practical lighting.

checkpoints.title: Polarity and power
checkpoints.practice:
On the bench, with clips.

1. Find plus and minus on the strip.
2. Connect it to the supply, correctly.
3. Then disconnect and reverse it deliberately, and observe that nothing happens and nothing is damaged.
4. Then back the right way round.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify polarity correctly on varied strip samples.

checkpoints.title: Cut it properly
checkpoints.practice:
Cut a strip to a length you need.

1. Find the cut line and cut exactly on it.
2. Both halves should have complete pads.
3. Fit a clip connector to each cut end and prove both halves still work.
checkpoints.criteria: Make a permitted cut leaving both sections functional and pads intact.

checkpoints.title: Put it inside something
checkpoints.practice:
A printed object with the strip inside it.

1. Design or choose something with a cavity or a channel.
2. Strip hidden, light coming out where you want it.
3. Wires routed out somewhere sensible.
4. A switch.
checkpoints.criteria: Install lighting so the intended viewer sees illumination without exposed LEDs.

checkpoints.title: Make it live somewhere
checkpoints.practice:
Put it where it will actually be used. A shelf, a desk, a doorway, a sign.

Then leave it a week and see whether it is still on and still liked.
checkpoints.criteria: Have the installation remain in use for a week.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Plain strip stock and the low-voltage supply bench.

skills.title: First glow
skills.objective: Understand addressable LED wiring and direction, explore effects, and light a bench strip.

checkpoints.title: The three wires
checkpoints.practice: On a bench strip, point at power, ground and data, and show which end is IN.
checkpoints.criteria: Find and interpret the data-direction arrow on varied strips.

checkpoints.title: Seven moods

checkpoints.practice: Wire a short strip to a bench supply and brain per the sheet. No solder, all clips.
checkpoints.criteria: Run the test pattern successfully after checking direction before power.

skills.objective: Estimate LED demand, compare it with supply capacity, and verify actual consumption.

checkpoints.title: The multiplication
checkpoints.practice: We give you three imaginary projects. You budget them.
checkpoints.criteria: Apply the lesson's LED-demand calculation and judge the supplied examples.

checkpoints.title: Prove it with the meter
checkpoints.practice: Bench strip, bench meter. Measure the real current at full white, then at half brightness, then running Chase.
checkpoints.criteria: Record three measured results and explain the effects' relative consumption.
