skills.title: Solder a strip
skills.objective: Make reliable soldered LED-strip joins, corners, insulation, and strain relief.

checkpoints.title: Six clean joints
checkpoints.practice:
On scrap strip, six wires onto six pads.

Tin, tin, join. In and out.

Look at all six under the lens.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce six sound joints without shorts, lifted pads, or heat damage.

checkpoints.title: Join two sections
checkpoints.practice:
Two lengths of strip, joined with wires, and both lighting correctly.

1. Check the arrow direction on both before you start.
2. Wires the same length, kept short.
3. Power, ground and data in the right order.
4. Test before sleeving.
checkpoints.criteria: Join two sections that run the pattern together after your checks.

checkpoints.title: Turn a corner
checkpoints.practice:
A ninety degree corner, done properly.

Short wires, neat, strain relieved, sleeved.

Then flex the corner twenty times and test again.
checkpoints.criteria: Make a corner that survives flexing without loading the solder joints.

checkpoints.title: A run that lasts
checkpoints.practice:
Build a real run for a real place. At least two joints and a corner.

1. Soldered, sleeved, strain relieved.
2. Fed from the right end, and from both ends if it is long.
3. Mounted so nothing pulls on a joint.
4. Then left running for a week.
checkpoints.criteria: Keep the installed run fully working for seven days.

skills.title: Write a pattern
skills.objective: Storyboard, implement, measure, and refine a custom lighting effect.

checkpoints.title: Describe before you build
checkpoints.practice:
Write your effect in one sentence, then storyboard it.

1. One sentence: what it does and what it is for.
2. Four boxes drawn on paper showing the strip at four moments.
3. The colour, brightness and speed written next to each box.
checkpoints.criteria: Provide a description and storyboard another person can interpret.

checkpoints.title: Build it
checkpoints.practice:
In the Arduino IDE, with the FastLED library on a Nano or an ESP32. Open File, Examples, FastLED, DemoReel100 and read how one of those patterns works before you write yours.

Then compare it with your storyboard and fix the differences.

It will be faster and brighter than you drew. Everybody's is.
checkpoints.criteria: Match the built effect to the storyboard and intended speed.

checkpoints.title: Measure what it costs
checkpoints.practice:
Meter on the supply.

1. Measure the current at the effect's quietest moment.
2. Measure it at the busiest moment.
3. Then measure full white at full brightness for comparison.
4. Three numbers. Now you know what your effect costs and what the ceiling is.
checkpoints.criteria: Record three power figures and compare actual demand with the maximum.

checkpoints.title: The ten minute test
checkpoints.practice:
Run it for ten minutes while you do something else in the same room.

Then decide honestly whether you would want it on a shelf at home.

Almost everybody slows theirs down and takes something out at this point.
checkpoints.criteria: Run for ten minutes and make a justified improvement.

checkpoints.title: The plan
checkpoints.practice: One sheet: what gets lit, where the strip hides, where power comes from, and the multiplication.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete all four required planning items before cutting wire.

checkpoints.title: You see light, not lights
checkpoints.practice: Build it.
checkpoints.criteria: Conceal direct LEDs from the intended viewing position.

checkpoints.title: It survives the shelf
checkpoints.practice: The piece goes on the display shelf, lit, for a week.
checkpoints.criteria: Keep the finished piece working for seven days without intervention.

skills.title: Diffusers and channels
skills.objective: Compare diffuser materials and spacing, design matching channels, and publish reusable profiles.

checkpoints.title: Print the test ladder
checkpoints.practice:
Same diffuser profile, four wall thicknesses.

Light all four with the same strip at the same distance.

Photograph them together and judge them side by side, not one at a time.
checkpoints.criteria: Determine a suitable wall thickness using a printed comparison ladder.

checkpoints.title: Prove distance matters more
checkpoints.practice:
Take your best diffuser and vary the gap instead.

5mm, 10mm, 15mm, 20mm.

Then compare against the wall thickness test.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate the effect of distance and explain its tradeoff.

checkpoints.title: Design a channel pair
checkpoints.practice:
A channel and a diffuser that fit together.

1. Strip sits straight and cannot move.
2. Diffuser slides in and stays without glue.
3. Interior blacked where light should not go.
4. End caps.
5. Designed for the machine, printed without supports.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce hand-assembled channels that retain correctly and control light leakage.

checkpoints.title: Put it in the print library
checkpoints.practice:
Make it useful to other people.

1. Parametric if you can, so it can be resized.
2. Named clearly with the strip width it fits.
3. A note: filament, wall count, infill, print orientation, and the LED gap it is designed for.
4. Include your test ladder findings.
checkpoints.criteria: Have another person print and use the channel successfully on the first try.

skills.title: Wled and the esp32
skills.objective: Install WLED on an ESP32, configure limits, wire strips, and enable phone control.

checkpoints.title: Flash and configure
checkpoints.practice:
Board flashed, on the network, configured.

1. Named so somebody else knows what and where it is.
2. LED count set to the real number.
3. Current limit set to what your supply can actually deliver.
4. Data pin set to match your wiring.
checkpoints.criteria: Reach the controller from a phone with correct strip length and limits.

checkpoints.title: Wire it safely
checkpoints.practice:
Supply to strip, supply to board, grounds joined, data to the arrow tail.

Then meter it: supply voltage under load, and current at full white with the limit on.

The limit should hold the current below your supply's rating.
checkpoints.criteria: Measure full-white demand below the supply rating with limiting active.

checkpoints.title: Drive it from a phone
checkpoints.practice:
Hand your phone to somebody who has never seen it.

They should be able to change the colour, change the effect, and turn it off, without instructions.
checkpoints.criteria: Let a first-time user change the lighting independently.

checkpoints.title: Make it live somewhere
checkpoints.practice:
Install it properly.

1. Controller in an enclosure, not loose on a shelf.
2. Supply secured, cables strain relieved.
3. Labelled: what it drives, what it is called, how many LEDs, what supply.
4. Left running for a week.
checkpoints.criteria: Run for a week with use by another person.

skills.title: Program the room
skills.objective: Map lighting segments, name presets, schedule shows, and hand over event operation.

checkpoints.title: Segment it
checkpoints.practice:
One physical run, at least three segments, each doing something different.

Then prove they are independent: change one and watch the others carry on.
checkpoints.criteria: Control three correctly mapped segments independently.

checkpoints.title: Build a preset set
checkpoints.practice:
At least six presets that cover the real situations:

1. Normal working light.
2. Arrival, for when people come in.
3. Something for a demonstration, calm and not distracting.
4. Something loud for a moment that deserves it.
5. Winding down.
6. Off.
checkpoints.criteria: Create six named presets another person can choose appropriately.

checkpoints.title: A show that runs itself
checkpoints.practice:
A playlist for a real event, with durations.

1. Ordered so it builds and settles rather than being uniformly busy.
2. Timed to the actual length of the event.
3. Ending somewhere sensible.
4. Scheduled to start and stop by itself.
checkpoints.criteria: Run a real event from its programmed schedule without intervention.

checkpoints.title: Hand it over
checkpoints.practice:
Somebody else has to be able to run it when you are not here.

1. Write the one page: what the controller is called, how to reach it, what the presets are for, and how to get back to normal.
2. Show one person.
3. Then be absent for an event and see whether it worked.
checkpoints.criteria: Have an event run correctly while you are absent.

skills.title: The matrix
skills.objective: Map a two-dimensional LED panel, budget power, and create readable animated signage.

checkpoints.title: Map it
checkpoints.practice:
Before anything else.

1. Light LED zero and find it.
2. Step through one at a time and watch the path.
3. Draw the mapping on squared paper.
4. Configure the controller to match, then test with a diagonal line.
5. A diagonal is the perfect test. Any mapping error turns it into a staircase or a zigzag immediately.
checkpoints.criteria: Render a straight corner-to-corner diagonal through correct mapping.

checkpoints.title: Power it safely
checkpoints.practice:
Budget it before you plug it in.

1. Count the LEDs, multiply by sixty, and write the full white figure down.
2. Compare with your supply and set the current limit accordingly.
3. Wire the injection points with wire heavy enough for the current.
4. Then, with the limit set, go to full white and meter it.
checkpoints.criteria: Confirm measured full-white current stays within the predicted supply limit.

checkpoints.title: Show something
checkpoints.practice:
Text, an image and a short animation.

1. Text that is readable from across the room.
2. An image designed at the panel's real size.
3. An animation that is not just an effect: something that means something.
checkpoints.criteria: Display all three required examples legibly across the room.

checkpoints.title: Make a real sign
checkpoints.practice:
Something the workshop or somebody actually wants.

1. Housed, diffused, and mounted.
2. Content that changes for a reason: open and closed, an event, a countdown, a name.
3. Powered safely and labelled.
4. Left running for a week.
checkpoints.criteria: Install a sign that another person reads and acts on.

skills.title: The installation
skills.objective: Survey, build, commission, document, and maintain a permanent lighting installation.

checkpoints.title: Survey and propose
checkpoints.practice:
One sheet, before anything is bought or cut.

1. Who wants it and what for.
2. The site: measurements, power, mounting, obstacles.
3. The design: what the light does, in one sentence, plus a sketch.
4. The numbers: LED count, current at full, supply chosen, with headroom.
5. How it is controlled and by whom.
6. What happens when it fails.
checkpoints.criteria: Obtain staff approval for a complete proposal, power plan, and mounting.

checkpoints.title: Build it to standard
checkpoints.practice:
Every joint soldered and sleeved. Everything secured. Everything labelled.

Then inspect your own work before you ask us to.

Photograph the wiring before you close anything up. You will want those photographs later and so will the next person.
checkpoints.criteria: Pass installation inspection with secure cables and complete labeling.

checkpoints.title: Commission it
checkpoints.practice:
Bring it into service properly.

1. Presets built and named for the real situations.
2. Schedule set and tested by changing the clock.
3. Boot preset set, so a power cut recovers correctly.
4. Somebody who is not you shown how to use it and how to get back to normal.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate scheduled operation and recovery after a power interruption.

checkpoints.title: Document it
checkpoints.practice:
One page, where the next person will find it.

1. What it is and what it does.
2. Controller name and how to reach it.
3. LED count, supply, current limit.
4. Wiring photographs.
5. The presets and what they are for.
6. Known issues, and what to do first if it stops working.
7. Your name and the date.
checkpoints.criteria: Write a guide sufficient for another person to fix the likely fault.

checkpoints.title: A month in service
checkpoints.practice:
It stays up and it stays working.

Check it weekly. Fix what needs fixing. Note what you would change.

At the end of the month, write two paragraphs: what you would do differently, and what you would do again.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete thirty days in service and provide an honest review.

skills.title: Sanding and surface
skills.objective: Remove print remnants, progress through abrasives, wet-sand, and inspect surface quality.

checkpoints.title: Clean removal
checkpoints.practice:
Before any paper touches it.

1. Supports off. Use pliers, pull along the part not away from it
2. Brim off in one piece if you can
3. Trim the little stubs flush with a knife, cutting away from your hand
4. Look at where the supports were. That is the surface you are about to spend the most time on
checkpoints.criteria: Remove raised remnants that catch a fingernail.

checkpoints.title: Work the grades
checkpoints.practice:
Coarse to fine, never skipping.

A normal run is something like 120, then 240, then 400, then 800.

1. Start coarse enough to actually remove the layer lines
2. Sand in different directions between grades so you can see the old scratches disappearing
3. Move up only when the previous grade's marks are gone
4. Wipe the dust between grades or you are dragging grit around
checkpoints.criteria: Remove the previous abrasive grade's scratches at every step.

checkpoints.title: Wet sand
checkpoints.practice:
For the fine grades, water changes everything.

1. 400 and above, with water
2. Keep the paper and the part wet
3. Rinse the paper often. It clogs
4. Light pressure. The water and the paper do the work
5. Wet sanding cuts the dust, stops the paper loading up, and gets you a much smoother result for less effort.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a consistent surface when wet and dry.

checkpoints.title: Check it properly
checkpoints.practice:
Nearly everybody stops too early because they are looking at it wrong.

1. Dry it completely
2. Hold it under a light at a low angle and look ALONG the surface, not straight at it
3. Turn it. Every face, every angle
4. Mark anything you find with a pencil and go back
5. Curved and detailed areas are where everybody gives up. Those are the areas people look at.
checkpoints.criteria: Find an additional defect during a second inspection.

skills.title: Fill and smooth
skills.objective: Use primer and filler to reveal and remove seams, gaps, and visible layer lines.

checkpoints.title: Prime to see
checkpoints.practice:
Take a sanded part and put one thin coat of primer on it.

Then look at it under raking light and mark every fault you find with a pencil.

There will be more than you expect. That is the point of the checkpoint.
checkpoints.criteria: Reveal at least six defects on an apparently finished part.

checkpoints.title: Fill a real gap
checkpoints.practice:
A seam, a gap or a dent.

1. Putty proud of the surface.
2. Cure fully. Read the tin, and then wait a bit longer.
3. Sand back flush, working up the grits.
4. Prime and check in raking light.
checkpoints.criteria: Hide a filled gap under primer when viewed in raking light.

checkpoints.title: Kill the layer lines
checkpoints.practice:
One face, taken all the way.

Sand, filler primer, sand, filler primer, until the layer lines are completely gone.

Two or three loops is normal. One is not enough and everybody tries one first.
checkpoints.criteria: Remove visible layer lines and surface ridges from the selected face.

checkpoints.title: Decide what matters
checkpoints.practice:
On a real piece, decide which surfaces get the full treatment and which do not.

The face people see. The face people touch. The face nobody will ever look at.

Then spend your effort accordingly and say why.
checkpoints.criteria: Explain the chosen stopping point for the intended viewing angle.

skills.title: Priming and painting
skills.objective: Prepare, prime, paint, and protect printed objects to a finished standard.

checkpoints.title: Prep the part
checkpoints.practice:
Before any paint.

1. All supports and brim removed
2. Sand from coarse to fine, never skip grades
3. Wipe the dust off properly. A dry cloth does not do it
4. Hold it up to the light at an angle and look along the surface, not at it
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a surface without detectable steps or remnants.

checkpoints.title: Prime it
checkpoints.practice:
Primer is not paint. It is the layer that makes paint stick and shows you what you missed.

1. Mount the part on a stick or a clip so you never touch it
2. Booth, fan on, mask on
3. Shake it properly. Longer than you think
4. Hold it a hand span away and keep moving
5. Light passes. It should look barely covered after the first one
6. Let it dry between coats
checkpoints.criteria: Apply uniform primer and resolve defects it reveals.

checkpoints.title: Base coat
checkpoints.practice:
1. Same rules. Thin, moving, several passes
2. Work from the awkward bits outwards, not the easy face first
3. Do not go back over a coat that has started to dry. Leave it and do another coat later
checkpoints.criteria: Apply an even base coat without runs or fingerprints.

checkpoints.title: Finish and protect
checkpoints.practice:
1. Detail or second colour if your design has one. Mask properly, press the edge down hard
2. Let it cure. Dry and cured are not the same thing
3. Seal it, matt or gloss, your choice and you should be able to say why
4. Label it and shelf it with the date
checkpoints.criteria: Finish and protect the object for normal customer handling.

skills.title: Masking and clean edges
skills.objective: Mask flat and curved boundaries, correct defects selectively, and create clean two-color finishes.

checkpoints.title: A line on flat
checkpoints.practice:
A flat test panel, two colours.

1. Base coat, cured.
2. Tape, burnished at the edge.
3. Seal coat in the base colour, over the tape edge, thin.
4. Top colour, thin coats.
5. Tape off at the right moment, at an angle.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a crisp straight boundary without bleed or lifted paint.

checkpoints.title: A curve
checkpoints.practice:
Now a curved line on a curved surface.

Narrow tape to define the curve, wide tape to fill in behind.

Same seal coat trick.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a smooth curved boundary without tape creep or creases.

checkpoints.title: Touch up honestly
checkpoints.practice:
Find the imperfections in your own line and fix them with a fine brush.

Under magnification if you need it.

Then look at the whole piece from a normal viewing distance and decide whether you should have bothered.
checkpoints.criteria: Make the result read cleanly at normal distance and explain retained imperfections.

checkpoints.title: A real piece, two colours
checkpoints.practice:
Something you actually made, with a deliberate two colour scheme.

Not a stripe for the sake of it. A colour break that means something: a panel, a trim, a marking, a functional face.
checkpoints.criteria: Finish a real two-color piece with intentional, clean boundaries.

skills.title: Colour and palette
skills.objective: Plan color schemes, test dried samples, control visual ratios, and explain design choices.

checkpoints.title: Pick a scheme with a reason
checkpoints.practice:
Before you open anything.

Pick one of these and name it:

MONOCHROME One colour, light to dark. Hard to get wrong, always looks deliberate.

COMPLEMENTARY Two colours from opposite sides of the wheel. High contrast, strong, easy to overdo.

ANALOGOUS Three colours sitting next to each other. Calm and cohesive.

ACCENT One quiet base with a single loud colour used sparingly.
checkpoints.criteria: Name the scheme and explain the intended visual focal point.

checkpoints.title: Make a test card
checkpoints.practice:
Nobody can judge paint from the pot.

1. Sand and prime a flat offcut
2. Paint a patch of every colour you plan to use
3. Let them dry fully
4. Label each one
5. Hold it next to your actual piece
6. Keep your test cards. After a year you have a reference nobody else in the workshop has.
checkpoints.criteria: Prepare labeled dry samples on primed material.

checkpoints.title: Control the ratio
checkpoints.practice:
This is where the badge is actually won.

A working rule to start from:

1. About two thirds one main colour
2. About a quarter a secondary
3. A small amount of accent. Less than you want to use
4. The accent is the colour people remember, and it only works because there is so little of it.
checkpoints.criteria: Make the dominant color immediately identifiable to viewers.

checkpoints.title: Finish and defend it
checkpoints.practice:
1. Paint the piece to your scheme
2. Do not add a colour halfway through because you got bored
3. Present it and explain your choices
checkpoints.criteria: Justify both selected and deliberately omitted colors.

skills.title: Decals and markings
skills.objective: Design and apply consistent decals and markings on flat and curved surfaces.

checkpoints.title: Gloss, apply, seal
checkpoints.practice:
One decal, done correctly, on a test piece.

1. Gloss coat, cured.
2. Decal with setting solution.
3. Fully dry.
4. Sealed.
5. Then do a second one on a matt surface with no gloss coat, deliberately, so you can see silvering for yourself.
checkpoints.criteria: Show a clean decal and identify silvering on the comparison failure.

checkpoints.title: Design a marking set
checkpoints.practice:
Not one decal. A set that belongs together.

1. A logo or symbol.
2. A number or identifier.
3. A warning or informational marking.
4. All in a consistent style and readable at the real size.
checkpoints.criteria: Create a coherent marking set legible at its application size.

checkpoints.title: Apply over a curve
checkpoints.practice:
A decal onto a curved or panelled surface.

Setting solution, patience, and a cotton bud to work the air out.

A decal over a panel line needs to be cut into the line and settled either side.
checkpoints.criteria: Fit a decal over curves and panel details without visible defects.

checkpoints.title: Mark a real piece
checkpoints.practice:
Something you made, marked deliberately.

Fewer markings than you first wanted, placed where they mean something.

Then seal and finish the whole piece to a single consistent sheen.
checkpoints.criteria: Integrate markings so they appear part of the finished object.

skills.title: Detail and weathering
skills.objective: Use washes, dry brushing, and weathering to communicate form, material, and wear.

checkpoints.title: Wash the recesses
checkpoints.practice:
Thin dark paint that runs into the low spots.

1. Thin your dark colour heavily. More thinner than paint
2. Flow it into the recesses, do not scrub it on
3. Let it settle into the corners
4. Wipe the raised areas back before it dries, if you went too far
checkpoints.criteria: Darken recesses while preserving the main surface color.

checkpoints.title: Dry brush the edges
checkpoints.practice:
The opposite move.

1. Light colour on the brush
2. Wipe almost all of it off on kitchen roll. More than feels right
3. Flick the brush lightly across the raised edges
4. Build it up over several passes
5. If it is going on in a solid streak you have too much paint on the brush.
checkpoints.criteria: Highlight edges without visible individual brush strokes.

checkpoints.title: Wear and chipping
checkpoints.practice:
Where would this actually get worn?

1. Corners and edges that get handled
2. Feet and bases
3. Around anything that moves or opens
4. Not randomly all over
5. Use a sponge torn to a rough edge, barely any paint, and dab.
6. Think about the object first. A hammer wears on the head. A box wears on the lid edge and the corners.
checkpoints.criteria: Explain why each worn area would occur in that location.

checkpoints.title: Know when to stop
checkpoints.practice:
The hardest checkpoint in the Art pathway.

1. Do the work
2. Put it down
3. Leave it until your next session
4. Look again and decide whether it needs anything
5. Most pieces need nothing. Some need one small thing. Almost none need everything you were about to do.
checkpoints.criteria: Reassess a piece next session and justify adding nothing further.

skills.title: Faux finishes
skills.objective: Use texture and paint to imitate metal and other materials on printed parts.

checkpoints.title: Texture first
checkpoints.practice:
Three test panels, three textures, no colour at all.

Stipple, drag and sponge. Then look at them in raking light and see how differently they behave.

Then prime all three the same grey and look again.
checkpoints.criteria: Create three visibly different textures beneath the same color.

checkpoints.title: One convincing metal
checkpoints.practice:
Pick one: cast iron, brass, or steel.

Reference object on the bench beside you the whole time.

1. Texture.
2. Dark base.
3. Metallic on the raised parts only.
4. Wash into the recesses.
5. Polish where a hand would touch.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a metal finish convincing enough to prompt physical inspection.

checkpoints.title: A second material
checkpoints.practice:
A completely different one. Wood, stone, or rust.

Same discipline: reference, texture, base, modulate, finish.

And the specific rule of that material: grain direction for wood, gravity for rust, value for stone.
checkpoints.criteria: Make a second material equally convincing through its own surface rules.

checkpoints.title: Two materials on one piece
checkpoints.practice:
The real test. One object, two materials meeting.

A wooden handle on an iron tool. A brass fitting on a stone base.

The join has to be believable, which usually means a little of each material's dirt crossing onto the other.
checkpoints.criteria: Combine two readable materials with a believable junction.

skills.title: Bases and plinths
skills.objective: Choose proportional plinths, mount securely, and finish bases that support the main object.

checkpoints.title: Proportion study
checkpoints.practice:
Print or cut three bases for the same piece at three sizes.

Stand the piece on each one and photograph all three from the same angle.

Then choose, and say why.
checkpoints.criteria: Defend the selected base proportions with design reasoning.

checkpoints.title: Mount it properly
checkpoints.practice:
Pinned or rodded, not just glued.

1. Drill the piece and the base to match.
2. Dry fit and check it is level.
3. Fix it, and let it cure fully.
4. Then pick the whole thing up by the piece, gently, and see whether you trust it.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a secure, level mounting that withstands the specified handling test.

checkpoints.title: Finish the base
checkpoints.practice:
The base gets the full Art treatment, at a lower intensity than the piece.

1. Sanded and filled, same as any part.
2. Painted or finished so it contrasts with the piece.
3. Underside finished: felt, or a printed foot, and no rocking.
4. A plaque.
checkpoints.criteria: Finish every base face and eliminate rocking on a flat surface.

checkpoints.title: See if it disappears
checkpoints.practice:
Put it in front of people and watch what they look at.

Ask them afterwards to describe the piece. If they mention the base unprompted, the base is competing.
checkpoints.criteria: Have viewers focus on the object while the base supports its presentation.

skills.title: Product photography
skills.objective: Light, frame, and photograph finished work with clean backgrounds and usable detail.

checkpoints.title: Light it
checkpoints.practice:
The one that matters most.

1. Big soft light from the side, not from the front
2. Never the phone flash. Never
3. A window on an overcast day is free and excellent
4. Bounce light back into the shadow side with white card
5. Watch what the light does to the edges. Side light shows shape, front light flattens it
checkpoints.criteria: Show directional lighting while preserving shadow detail.

checkpoints.title: Background and surface
checkpoints.practice:
Everything behind the piece is competing with it.

1. Plain. One colour
2. Not the bench, not the cutting mat, not a pile of tools
3. No hard line where the surface meets the wall. Curve the paper up behind
4. Contrast with the piece. Dark object, light background
checkpoints.criteria: Keep the frame free of distractions beyond the object and plain surface.

checkpoints.title: Angle and frame
checkpoints.practice:
1. Camera at the object's height, not looking down from standing
2. Slightly off to one side. Straight on is flat, three quarters shows form
3. Fill the frame. Get closer than feels right
4. Level. A tilted horizon reads as an accident
5. Take the detail shot too. The bit you are proudest of
checkpoints.criteria: Create worthwhile overall and detail views.

checkpoints.title: Deliver three
checkpoints.practice:
The real job.

1. Three finished photos of one piece
2. A hero shot, a different angle, and a detail
3. Cropped straight and level
4. Named properly with your name and what it is
5. Handed over the way we ask for them
checkpoints.criteria: Deliver three photographs usable without further editing.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: The photo bench and credited publication of workshop work.

skills.title: Display and presentation
skills.objective: Design stable display mounts, label the work, and install a finished piece publicly.

checkpoints.title: Design the base
checkpoints.practice:
The base is part of the piece, not a leftover.

1. Big enough that it will not tip
2. Not so big it dwarfs the object
3. Finished to the same standard as the piece. A beautiful model on a rough base looks worse than no base
4. Consider the material. A contrasting colour or finish separates the object from the surface
checkpoints.criteria: Make a base stable under the prescribed gentle test.

checkpoints.title: Mount it properly
checkpoints.practice:
It has to survive being picked up by somebody who does not know how it is put together.

1. Mechanical first. A pin, a peg, a socket. Glue alone is not mounting
2. Glue as well, in the right place
3. Nothing visible from the front
4. Let it cure fully before you handle it
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate a secure connection between object and base.

checkpoints.title: Label it
checkpoints.practice:
Nobody knows what they are looking at unless you tell them.

1. What it is
2. Who made it. Your first name
3. When
4. One line about it. The material, the technique, the idea. Short
5. Print it or make it, but make it match the piece. A laser engraved plate on a weathered piece, a printed card on a clean one.
checkpoints.criteria: Write a label understandable to a new visitor.

checkpoints.title: Put it on the shelf
checkpoints.practice:
The last step, and it is a real one.

1. Photograph it properly. You have a badge for that
2. Bring it to us finished, mounted and labelled
3. We put it out
4. It stays out
5. If it comes back damaged from being handled, that is information. Fix it and put it back.
checkpoints.criteria: Display the work for a week without failure.

skills.title: Press record
skills.objective: Obtain filming permission, capture steady footage, improve light, and cover workshop events.

checkpoints.title: Ask properly
checkpoints.practice:
Film something on the workshop floor that includes another person.

Ask them first, explain what it is for, and tell them what happens to the footage.

Then do it again with somebody who might say no.
checkpoints.criteria: Ask three people appropriately and respectfully handle at least one refusal.

checkpoints.title: Five shots that hold
checkpoints.practice:
Five different shots of the same activity.

1. Wide, showing where it is.
2. Mid, showing the person working.
3. Close, showing the hands.
4. Very close, showing the detail that matters.
5. One from an unexpected angle: low, high, or through something.
6. Every one on a tripod or properly braced, and every one held for at least ten seconds.
checkpoints.criteria: Record five steady, sufficiently long, usable shots.

checkpoints.title: Fix the light
checkpoints.practice:
Film the same thing three ways:

1. With a bright window behind it.
2. With the light in front of it.
3. With a lamp moved deliberately to where you want it.
4. Then look at all three and see what light actually does.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify camera position and lighting changes before recording.

checkpoints.title: Cover an event
checkpoints.practice:
Something real happening in the workshop. A build, a launch, a derby, a screening.

Come away with enough footage that somebody could edit it without you.

That means wide, mid, close, and the moments either side of the important bit.
checkpoints.criteria: Capture enough coherent coverage for an editor who missed the event.

skills.title: Get the sound right
skills.objective: Choose microphone placement, control room noise, set levels, and record clear speech.

checkpoints.title: Distance test
checkpoints.practice:
One person talking, recorded four times.

Two metres, one metre, half a metre, twenty centimetres.

Same everything else. Then listen to all four on headphones.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate the audible effect of microphone distance.

checkpoints.title: Kill the room
checkpoints.practice:
Record the same line in three places:

1. In the middle of the workshop with everything running.
2. In the same place with the extraction off.
3. In the quiet corner.
4. Then record thirty seconds of room tone in each.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify recorded noise sources and choose an appropriate room location.

checkpoints.title: Monitor and set levels
checkpoints.practice:
Headphones on, meter visible.

1. Set the level so speech peaks around two thirds.
2. Deliberately record something clipped, so you know what it sounds like and that it cannot be fixed.
3. Deliberately record something far too quiet and try to lift it, so you hear the hiss come up.
checkpoints.criteria: Set recording level within thirty seconds and recognize both failure types.

checkpoints.title: Record somebody properly
checkpoints.practice:
A real interview or a real explanation. Two minutes, usable.

1. Mic close and mounted.
2. Quiet location, extraction off.
3. Headphones on throughout.
4. Room tone recorded afterwards.
5. Level correct all the way through.
checkpoints.criteria: Deliver two minutes of clean audio requiring no repair.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.

skills.title: Make a cut
skills.objective: Shape a film around a clear idea, use smooth cuts, shorten it, and export a complete result.

checkpoints.title: The one sentence
checkpoints.practice:
Before touching the footage, write what the film is in one sentence and list the three things it must show.

Then review your footage and mark only the shots that serve those three things.
checkpoints.criteria: Select footage that supports one stated idea and omit distracting favorites.

checkpoints.title: Cut on action
checkpoints.practice:
Take two shots of the same movement from different angles.

Cut between them in the middle of the movement.

Then cut the same two before and after the movement, and compare.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate a clean action cut and explain a less effective alternative.

checkpoints.title: Make it shorter
checkpoints.practice:
Get a rough cut to a length you are happy with.

Then cut a third out of it.

Then watch both, all the way through, without stopping.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce a shorter edit that improves the film.

checkpoints.title: Finish it
checkpoints.practice:
A finished short piece. Two minutes or under.

1. Title at the start, readable on a phone.
2. Clean audio throughout, with room tone under any gaps.
3. Credits at the end, including everybody who appears in it.
4. Exported properly and playable on a phone, a laptop and a television.
checkpoints.criteria: Have another person voluntarily watch the finished film to the end.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: The editing bench and footage storage on the project drive.

skills.title: The timelapse
skills.objective: Calculate timelapse timing, lock camera settings, capture a complete sequence, and edit it.

checkpoints.title: Do the arithmetic
checkpoints.practice:
For a real job:

1. Length of the event in seconds.
2. Desired finished length in seconds.
3. Frames needed.
4. Interval.
5. Write all four down before you set anything up.
checkpoints.criteria: Calculate the four timing figures and achieve approximately the planned duration.

checkpoints.title: Lock it all down
checkpoints.practice:
Everything manual, everything fixed.

Then take three frames five minutes apart and compare them for exposure, focus and colour.

If any of the three has shifted, something is still on automatic.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce three consistent test frames except for the intended movement.

checkpoints.title: Shoot a print
checkpoints.practice:
A real print, start to finish, unattended.

1. Camera mounted and out of the way.
2. Everything manual.
3. A note on the machine saying what is happening so nobody moves it.
4. Power sorted.
checkpoints.criteria: Capture a full print sequence without flicker, bumps, or gaps.

checkpoints.title: Cut it and show it
checkpoints.practice:
Assemble, trim the dead ends, add a title, and add sound.

Silence under a timelapse is uncomfortable. Room tone, music, or the printer's own sound slowed down.
checkpoints.criteria: Finish a sequence another person chooses to watch twice.

skills.title: Document a build
skills.objective: Plan and film an honest build story, including failure, diagnosis, repair, and audience feedback.

checkpoints.title: Plan the shoot
checkpoints.practice:
One sheet, against the build's stages.

1. Every stage listed, with dates.
2. What you will film at each one.
3. What you need: light, mic, tripod, a second pair of hands.
4. Who is in it and whether they have agreed.
checkpoints.criteria: Plan coverage for the whole build, including time-critical stages.

checkpoints.title: Film the failure
checkpoints.practice:
Something will go wrong. It always does.

Film it while it is happening or immediately after, before it is cleared away.

Then film the diagnosis and the fix.
checkpoints.criteria: Capture an actual failure, diagnosis, and repair in sequence.

checkpoints.title: Cut it
checkpoints.practice:
Three to five minutes, maximum.

The shape above. Captions for facts, voice only where it is needed.

Clean sound throughout.

Then show it to the person who did the build, before anybody else.
checkpoints.criteria: Make an edit the builder agrees represents the process fairly.

checkpoints.title: Show it to strangers
checkpoints.practice:
Play it to people who were not there and did not do the build.

Watch them, do not explain anything.

Note where they lose interest and where they lean in.
checkpoints.criteria: Observe three new viewers and revise the film based on their responses.

skills.title: Encode a reel
skills.objective: Choose an Atlas reel look, prepare readable cards, match loudness, and verify the encoded result.

checkpoints.title: Pick a look
checkpoints.practice:
One source, three looks, three thirty second previews.

Watch all three on a real Atlas, in normal workshop light.

Then choose, and say what you are trading.
checkpoints.criteria: Select the visual treatment from device previews and explain the tradeoff.

checkpoints.title: Get the cards right
checkpoints.practice:
A source with title cards or intertitles.

Check on the device that the text is crisp and readable, not dithered into grey mush.

If it is not, adjust and preview again.
checkpoints.criteria: Verify every title card is readable on an Atlas at arm's length.

checkpoints.title: Level the audio
checkpoints.practice:
Check the source loudness, and bring it to the shelf standard.

1. Read what the source measures.
2. Adjust to the target.
3. Listen to the loudest and quietest parts on headphones.
4. Then compare it against something already on the shelf, back to back on a device.
checkpoints.criteria: Match playback loudness to existing Library items.

checkpoints.title: Encode the whole thing
checkpoints.practice:
The full run, with your chosen settings.

Then watch the whole thing on a device. All of it. Not a sample.

Look for: cards you missed, a section where the look falls apart, audio drift, and the ending.
checkpoints.criteria: Watch the full encoded reel on hardware and resolve any faults.

skills.title: Put it on the shelf
skills.objective: Name and organize Library reels so their filenames and shelf order remain usable.

checkpoints.title: Name ten
checkpoints.practice:
We give you ten badly named files.

Rename them all to the convention, and keep the sidecars matched.

Then look at the result on a device.
checkpoints.criteria: Name ten reels clearly on hardware while preserving audio.

checkpoints.title: Find the truncation point
checkpoints.practice:
Work out, on the actual device, how many characters of a name you actually get.

Then test a name that is too long and see what a reader sees.

Write the number in your notebook and tell everybody else.
checkpoints.criteria: Measure the actual filename truncation limit and remain within it.

checkpoints.title: Put yours on
checkpoints.practice:
Your own reel onto the shelf, properly.

1. Named to the convention.
2. Sidecar matched.
3. Placed where it makes sense in the order.
4. Checked on a device by scrolling to it as a stranger would.
checkpoints.criteria: Publish a reel another person discovers through browsing.

checkpoints.title: Tidy the shelf
checkpoints.practice:
Go through the whole shelf and fix what does not read.

Report anything you cannot fix: a broken reel, a missing sidecar, something that should not be there.

Do not delete anything. Report it.
checkpoints.criteria: Make the shelf consistent and report a genuine problem.

skills.title: Run a screening
skills.objective: Prepare a screening, choose an audience-appropriate program, host it, and respond to the room.

checkpoints.title: Prepare properly
checkpoints.practice:
The whole pre flight, an hour before.

1. Every reel checked on a device today.
2. Every loaner charged and working.
3. Running times written down.
4. Programme and a shorter alternative decided.
checkpoints.criteria: Check the setup so the screening has no avoidable surprises.

checkpoints.title: Programme it
checkpoints.practice:
Build a programme for a specific real audience.

Write it out: what, how long, why in that order, and where the exit is if it is going badly.
checkpoints.criteria: Justify the program and running order for its audience.

checkpoints.title: Host it
checkpoints.practice:
Run a real screening for a real room.

1. Introduce it: what and how long.
2. Get everybody joined.
3. Leave it alone.
4. Watch the room.
checkpoints.criteria: Maintain audience engagement or recognize and respond to a problem.

checkpoints.title: Read the room and adjust
checkpoints.practice:
Sooner or later a choice will not land.

Notice it, cut it short gracefully, and move to the next thing without making it a moment.

Then afterwards, work out why it did not land.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate an appropriate early ending when the audience response warrants it.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Hosting of workshop and public open-day screenings.

skills.title: The shop film
skills.objective: Make a permission-cleared short film, validate it on Atlas, publish it, and host a screening.

checkpoints.title: The sentence and the permissions
checkpoints.practice:
One sentence saying what the film is about.

And a list of everybody who will appear, with their agreement, and parental permission where it is needed.

Both before you shoot anything substantial.
checkpoints.criteria: State the film's subject clearly and obtain all permissions.

checkpoints.title: Test the look early
checkpoints.practice:
Shoot half a day, then encode a preview and watch it on an Atlas.

Find out what survives the small screen and what does not.

Then change how you shoot the rest.
checkpoints.criteria: Change the filming approach based on an early device test.

checkpoints.title: Shoot and cut
checkpoints.practice:
The full film.

1. Shot across several sessions, with clean sound.
2. Cut to the sentence, five to ten minutes.
3. Titles legible on the device.
4. Everybody credited.
5. Show it to the people in it before anybody else.
checkpoints.criteria: Deliver an edit that satisfies its subject and participants.

checkpoints.title: Onto the shelf
checkpoints.practice:
Encode it properly, level the audio to the shelf standard, name it to the convention, place it.

Then browse the shelf as a stranger and find it.
checkpoints.criteria: Publish a correctly named, playable reel at consistent loudness.

checkpoints.title: Screen it
checkpoints.practice:
A real screening, hosted by you, of your own film.

1. Introduce it in one sentence.
2. Show it.
3. Then shut up and watch the room.
4. Afterwards, take questions and take criticism.
checkpoints.criteria: Screen the film to a voluntary audience and handle the response.

skills.title: Stock and supplies
skills.objective: Count stock, set replenishment levels, report shortages early, and prepare for build days.

checkpoints.title: Count it properly
checkpoints.practice:
A full count of one area of the stores.

1. Weigh every spool and record grams.
2. Count every consumable.
3. Write it all down on the sheet.
4. Compare against what the board says we have.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete an accurate count and find a real stock-record discrepancy.

checkpoints.title: Set the triggers
checkpoints.practice:
For ten items, work out and write a trigger level.

Ask how long each takes to arrive. Some things are next day and some are three weeks.

Then label the shelves.
checkpoints.criteria: Set ten visible reorder triggers with reasons.

checkpoints.title: Report before it hurts
checkpoints.practice:
Run the stock check for a fortnight.

Report anything at or below trigger, on the board, in writing, on the day you find it.

Never at zero. Zero means you were too late.
checkpoints.criteria: Maintain two weeks without an unreported stockout.

checkpoints.title: Predict a build day
checkpoints.practice:
Take a real upcoming session or build day.

Work out what it will consume: filament, fasteners, cells, consumables.

Then check whether we have it, and order what we do not, before the day.
checkpoints.criteria: Prepare a build day without predictable supply shortages.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Use of the stock board and purchasing list.

skills.title: The machine log
skills.objective: Keep useful machine records, detect patterns, remove unsafe equipment, and run maintenance schedules.

checkpoints.title: Write ten entries
checkpoints.practice:
Over a fortnight, log ten real events across the machines.

Maintenance, faults, observations, and at least two entries that say everything was fine, because those matter too.
checkpoints.criteria: Write ten specific entries another person can understand.

checkpoints.title: Find a pattern
checkpoints.practice:
Read the logs back, all machines, three months.

Find something: a repeat, a drift, a correlation, or a machine nobody has logged.

Then say what you would do about it.
checkpoints.criteria: Identify a real trend and propose a practical response.

checkpoints.title: Tag one out
checkpoints.practice:
A machine that should not be in service.

1. Tag it, physically, with what is wrong and your name.
2. Log it.
3. Tell whoever is running the queue.
4. Then follow it up until it is fixed and the tag is signed off.
checkpoints.criteria: Keep a faulty machine out of use until properly repaired.

checkpoints.title: Run the rota
checkpoints.practice:
Take the maintenance schedule for a month.

Do the scheduled jobs, log them, and chase the ones you cannot do yourself.

At the end, report which machine needs the most attention and why.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete and document a month of scheduled maintenance.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: The maintenance schedule and authority to remove machines from service.

skills.title: Induct a newcomer
skills.objective: Observe and lead newcomer inductions, covering safety and a successful first making session.

checkpoints.title: Shadow two
checkpoints.practice:
Watch a staff member run two inductions, all the way through.

Write down what they said, in what order, and what they left out.

Then compare against what you would have said.
checkpoints.criteria: Observe two inductions and explain their scope and deliberate omissions.

checkpoints.title: Run the safety walk
checkpoints.practice:
The safety half only, with a staff member watching.

1. Walked, not described.
2. They point at the five things, you do not.
3. The four rules, in their words back to you.
4. Explain to your instructor straight away, explained with a real example.
checkpoints.criteria: Teach the safety tour so the newcomer identifies all five points unaided.

checkpoints.title: Get them making
checkpoints.practice:
Within the first hour, they are working on something.

It does not matter what. A nameplate, a paper rocket, a breadboard LED, a Maker pack.

It has to be theirs and it has to be finishable today.
checkpoints.criteria: Have the newcomer finish the first session with something they made.

checkpoints.title: Run five on your own
checkpoints.practice:
Five real inductions, staff nearby but not helping.

Different ages, different confidence levels, different reasons for being here.

Adjust for each of them.
checkpoints.criteria: Lead five inductions independently with at least four second-session returns.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Responsibility for workshop newcomer inductions.

skills.title: Quote a job
skills.objective: Estimate total job costs, measure hidden labor, quote realistic ranges, and communicate limits.

checkpoints.title: Cost a job you already did
checkpoints.practice:
Take a job that has already been done.

1. Material from the slicer, converted to money.
2. Machine hours, converted to money.
3. Your honest labour time, including everything after the print.
4. Then compare with what was actually charged.
checkpoints.criteria: Reconcile an estimate for a completed job with its actual cost.

checkpoints.title: Time the hidden work
checkpoints.practice:
Actually time it, with a stopwatch, on three real jobs:

1. Setup and slicing.
2. Support removal.
3. Sanding and finishing.
4. Packing and handover.
5. Write down the real numbers. They will be bigger than your estimate.
checkpoints.criteria: Time three jobs and derive a defensible post-processing allowance.

checkpoints.title: Quote three live
checkpoints.practice:
Three real requests, quoted by you before the work happens.

Include a range where you are unsure, and say what drives each end.

Then do the jobs and compare.
checkpoints.criteria: Produce three live quotes whose ranges contain the actual costs.

checkpoints.title: Say no properly
checkpoints.practice:
Sooner or later you will be asked for something where the honest quote is more than the person wants to pay.

1. Say the number, plainly.
2. Say what drives it.
3. Offer the cheaper version if there is one: different material, lower detail, fewer, or a redesign.
4. Do not quietly do it cheaper and absorb it yourself.
checkpoints.criteria: Communicate an unwelcome but honest quote professionally.

skills.preparation: Review prerequisites, collect the tools and materials for the task, and agree on a safe work area with the instructor.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Preparation of workshop quotes used for real customer invoices.

skills.title: Run a workshop
skills.objective: Plan, prepare, teach, time, and recover a practical group workshop.

checkpoints.title: Plan it on a card
checkpoints.practice:
One skill, from a badge you hold.

One card: skill, outcome, timings, cuts, failures.

Then walk the whole thing through in your head against a clock.
checkpoints.criteria: Create a complete plan that fits the slot and identifies optional cuts.

checkpoints.title: Prep the stations
checkpoints.practice:
Before anybody arrives.

1. Six identical sets of materials, laid out.
2. Two spares.
3. Tools at each station, not in a pile in the middle.
4. Your own demonstration piece, half finished, ready.
5. Bin, cloth and a place for finished work.
checkpoints.criteria: Prepare each station so a learner can begin immediately.

checkpoints.title: Run one
checkpoints.practice:
Thirty minutes, six people, real.

1. Doing something within five minutes.
2. Hands off their work.
3. Watch the clock.
4. Everybody leaves with the thing.
checkpoints.criteria: Finish on time with all six participants completing an object.

checkpoints.title: Run one that goes wrong
checkpoints.practice:
It will. Something breaks, somebody is upset, a station fails, you run out of a material.

Recover it without stopping the room.

Then afterwards, write down what you would change.
checkpoints.criteria: Handle a disrupted workshop while retaining completed outcomes and an honest review.

skills.preparation: Review prerequisites, collect the tools and materials for the task, and agree on a safe work area with the instructor.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Named workshop slots on the timetable.

skills.title: The market table
skills.objective: Make consistent batches, price products, present a market table, and learn from sales.

checkpoints.title: Make one, then make five
checkpoints.practice:
Time every stage of the first one.

Then make five and time those.

Find the bottleneck and improve it.

Then compare unit five with unit one for quality.
checkpoints.criteria: Make five units faster per item without reducing quality and identify the bottleneck.

checkpoints.title: Price it honestly
checkpoints.practice:
Full cost per unit, written out.

Then your price, with the margin shown.

Then ask five people what they would pay, before you tell them your number.
checkpoints.criteria: Set a price covering costs and compare it with customer responses.

checkpoints.title: Build the table
checkpoints.practice:
Set up your section properly.

1. Cloth, levels, and your best piece at eye height.
2. Clear prices. Every item, visible, no asking.
3. A sign with your name and what this is.
4. A photograph or two of the work being made, because people buy the making as much as the object.
checkpoints.criteria: Present products and prices clearly to passing visitors.

checkpoints.title: Stand behind it
checkpoints.practice:
A real market day or open day.

1. Be there, standing, not sitting behind a phone.
2. Let people pick things up.
3. Answer questions honestly, including how long it took and what it is made of.
4. Do not chase people.
5. Then count what sold, and what got picked up and put down. Both are data.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete a selling session, make a sale, and compare interest with purchases.

skills.preparation: Review prerequisites, collect the tools and materials for the task, and agree on a safe work area with the instructor.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: A selling space on the workshop market table with credited work.

skills.title: The real job
skills.objective: Manage customer work from an agreed brief and quote through delivery, payment, and follow-up.

checkpoints.title: Take and confirm a brief
checkpoints.practice:
A real request from a real customer, with a staff member present.

1. Ask what it is for before you ask what it looks like.
2. Measure anything it has to fit, yourself.
3. Agree what done means.
4. Write it up and send it back to them to confirm.
checkpoints.criteria: Agree a written brief that captures an initially unstated need.

checkpoints.title: Quote and schedule
checkpoints.practice:
A written quote, using everything from Quote A Job.

And a schedule with slack in it. If it needs four sessions, promise five.

Both agreed before you start.
checkpoints.criteria: Prepare an honest quote and schedule with genuine contingency.

checkpoints.title: Make it and check it
checkpoints.practice:
Do the work to the standard.

Then check it against the written brief, item by item, before you tell anybody it is ready.

Anything that does not match, you fix or you flag before delivery, never after.
checkpoints.criteria: Meet every brief requirement at a customer-ready finish standard.

checkpoints.title: Deliver and follow up
checkpoints.practice:
Hand it over with the invoice, in person where you can.

Ask them to look at it while you are there.

Then a week later, ask how it is going.
checkpoints.criteria: Deliver, receive payment, and confirm satisfaction a week later.

checkpoints.title: Handle something going wrong
checkpoints.practice:
Something will. A failed print, a wrong measurement, a delay.

1. Tell them the moment you know.
2. Say what happened, without excuses and without drama.
3. Say what you are doing about it and give a new date.
4. Then hit that date.
checkpoints.criteria: Communicate a problem early while still completing the job successfully.

skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Assignment of paid workshop jobs with personal responsibility recorded.

skills.title: Safety officer
skills.objective: Inspect workshop safety, report findings, intervene respectfully, and prevent repeated incidents.

checkpoints.title: Learn the list
checkpoints.practice:
Walk the full inspection with a staff member, twice.

Every item, including pressing every emergency stop and checking every extinguisher date.

Ask what each item is for. Every one exists because of something.
checkpoints.criteria: Perform the whole inspection unaided and explain its checks.

checkpoints.title: Inspect and report
checkpoints.practice:
Four weekly inspections, done alone, written up.

1. Every item checked, not skimmed.
2. Findings written, with what you did about each.
3. Anything you could not fix escalated in writing.
4. Never a clean sheet. There is always something, and a clean sheet means you did not look.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete four honest inspections and uncover a previously unknown issue.

checkpoints.title: Stop something
checkpoints.practice: Practise a respectful stop-work intervention in an instructor-led scenario. Explain the concern, notify the responsible staff member, and record the response. A real incident may be discussed if one already occurred; never create an unsafe event for assessment.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate and document a respectful stop-work intervention in a scenario or an already-occurring incident.

checkpoints.title: Stop somebody senior
checkpoints.practice: Role-play reporting a concern to a more senior person. Use clear, factual language and the academy escalation route. Explain how you would keep people clear while waiting for the responsible instructor.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrate the appropriate escalation to a more senior person in a supervised scenario.

checkpoints.title: Improve something
checkpoints.practice:
The part that makes it a capstone.

Find a recurring risk and change the workshop so it stops happening. Not a rule. A change.

A different storage position, a guard, a sign, a jig, a habit built into a procedure.

Then check in a month whether it worked.
checkpoints.criteria: Show in the incident records that a recurring issue has stopped.

skills.preparation: Review prerequisites, collect the tools and materials for the task, and agree on a safe work area with the instructor.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: An instructor observes the demonstration and records evidence before awarding this skill.
skills.unlocks: Staff-backed authority to stop unsafe workshop activity.

skills.title: Junior mentor
skills.objective: Support a staff-led bench, notice learners' needs, and maintain standards without taking over.

checkpoints.title: Be asked
checkpoints.practice:
This one is not yours to complete.

Staff put your name forward, after watching. Usually the trigger is that we notice we are already relying on you.

If you want it, the route is to be useful without being asked, repeatedly, over a term.
checkpoints.criteria: Receive a staff invitation based on observed readiness.

checkpoints.title: Run a bench beside us
checkpoints.practice:
Six sessions, at a bench, as the second pair of eyes.

1. Set up before, close down after.
2. Take the first question.
3. Hands off.
4. Report what you saw at the end of each session.
checkpoints.criteria: Improve the running of a staff-supported bench across six sessions.

checkpoints.title: Hold the line once
checkpoints.practice:
Sooner or later somebody will push. Ask you to do it for them, ask you to bend a rule, ask you to sign something off you cannot.

You hold the line and you stay pleasant about it.
checkpoints.criteria: Correctly uphold a standard with someone you like.

skills.preparation: Review prerequisites, collect the tools and materials for the task, and agree on a safe work area with the instructor.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: All ladder ranks are appointed through staff observation. Completing checkpoints alone does not guarantee a rank.
skills.unlocks: An appointed floor role assisting staff and helping newcomers.

skills.title: Specialist
skills.objective: Become a recognized discipline expert who maintains the bench standard and coaches others.

checkpoints.title: Hold a capstone
checkpoints.practice:
Any one of them, properly earned.

Not nearly. Signed.
checkpoints.criteria: Hold an eligible capstone recorded in the workshop passport.

checkpoints.title: Be the one they ask
checkpoints.practice:
Over a term, be the person the room turns to about your thing.

Not because we told them. Because you have answered well enough, often enough, that it became the obvious thing to do.
checkpoints.criteria: Be recognized by staff as someone learners already seek out.

checkpoints.title: Set the standard
checkpoints.practice:
Own the bench.

1. It is set up right when you are on the floor.
2. You say when somebody's work is not to standard, kindly and specifically.
3. You say when the workshop's own kit is not good enough. That is allowed and it is part of the job.
checkpoints.criteria: Demonstrably improve the discipline's bench standard.

checkpoints.title: Teach it
checkpoints.practice:
Take at least three people through a badge on your pathway, to a pass.

Not the same badge three times if you can help it. Spread it.
checkpoints.criteria: Coach three successful passes within the discipline.

skills.preparation: Review prerequisites, collect the tools and materials for the task, and agree on a safe work area with the instructor.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: Also requires an eligible capstone: BE-11, PR-12, DE-15, CI-13, AT-13, CO-16, SP-10, PI-11, LI-11, AR-11, ST-09, or OP-08. Staff must recognize an established discipline role.
skills.unlocks: Recognition as the first contact and trainer in a specialist discipline.

skills.title: Mentor
skills.objective: Run a bench independently, assess consistently, decline premature passes, and handle incidents.

checkpoints.title: Run it alone
checkpoints.practice:
A term of running a bench with staff on the floor but not at your shoulder.

Setup, session, close down, report.
checkpoints.criteria: Operate the bench safely with decreasing staff oversight.

checkpoints.title: Sign off consistently
checkpoints.practice:
Twenty sign offs across several people.

We will re assess some of them without telling you which.

Your standard should match ours, and it should match your own from a month earlier.
checkpoints.criteria: Have checkpoint sign-offs withstand staff consistency checks.

checkpoints.title: Fail somebody
checkpoints.practice:
The one everybody dreads.

Somebody you like will come to you nearly ready, wanting a pass.

You tell them what is missing, specifically, and what to do about it, and you do not sign.
checkpoints.criteria: Decline an incomplete assessment and support a later valid pass.

checkpoints.title: Handle something real
checkpoints.practice:
An injury, a serious near miss, a conflict between two people, or something breaking badly.

Handle the immediate part, escalate correctly, and write it up.

Then talk it through with us afterwards, honestly, including what you would do differently.
checkpoints.criteria: Handle and escalate a real incident, then review it honestly.

skills.preparation: Review prerequisites, collect the tools and materials for the task, and agree on a safe work area with the instructor.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: May assess only checkpoints on badges personally held. Staff retain oversight of standards.
skills.unlocks: Responsibility for a bench and sign-off authority on checkpoints for badges held.

skills.title: Lead hand
skills.objective: Plan and run whole sessions, circulate effectively, manage disruptions, and hand over clearly.

checkpoints.title: Plan a session
checkpoints.practice:
Before it starts, on one sheet:

1. Who is coming and what they are on.
2. What each will need, prepped.
3. What machines are needed and whether they are free.
4. Anything that could go wrong and what you will do.
checkpoints.criteria: Prepare a session that starts without participants waiting for supplies or setup.

checkpoints.title: Run six sessions
checkpoints.practice:
Six full sessions, staff in the building, not in the room.

Start on time, circulate, close on time, report.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete six well-run sessions with timely closing and a ready room.

checkpoints.title: Handle the thing that goes wrong
checkpoints.practice:
Something will. A failure, a conflict, a machine down, a parent arriving unhappy, somebody upset.

Handle the immediate, escalate correctly, keep the rest of the room running.
checkpoints.criteria: Keep the room operating while handling and promptly escalating an incident.

checkpoints.title: Hand over
checkpoints.practice:
Every session ends with a report that the next person can use.

Who did what, who needs what, what broke, what ran out, what to watch.

Six reports somebody actually used.
checkpoints.criteria: Write handovers another person can run a session from without questions.

skills.preparation: Review prerequisites, collect the tools and materials for the task, and agree on a safe work area with the instructor.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: Staff remain in the building. Six full sessions and usable handover reports are assessed.
skills.unlocks: Responsibility for scheduled sessions with staff available in the building.

skills.title: Apprentice
skills.objective: Sustain a reliable volunteer role, train successors, and make a lasting workshop contribution.

checkpoints.title: Be already doing it
checkpoints.practice:
The only real criterion.

By the time we offer this, you should be doing most of the job already, without the apron and without being asked.
checkpoints.criteria: Receive the role offer after already demonstrating its responsibilities.

checkpoints.title: Hold a rota
checkpoints.practice:
Shifts, agreed in advance, that people depend on.

1. You turn up.
2. If you cannot, you say so early and you help find cover.
3. You do the whole shift, including the closing.
checkpoints.criteria: Complete a term of agreed shifts without leaving others short.

checkpoints.title: Train your replacement
checkpoints.practice:
Bring somebody up the ladder behind you.

Peer Coaching to Junior Mentor at minimum. Further if you are here long enough.
checkpoints.criteria: Coach a successor who progresses to running a bench.

checkpoints.title: Make something we point at
checkpoints.practice:
A piece of work that lives here after you.

A design in the library. A film on the shelf. A mode in the firmware. An installation on the wall. A jig everybody uses. A rocket other people fly.

Something that outlasts your attention.
checkpoints.criteria: Create a lasting piece of work the workshop continues to use and show.

skills.preparation: Review prerequisites, collect the tools and materials for the task, and agree on a safe work area with the instructor.
skills.reflection: Explain what you changed, what evidence supports the result, and what you would improve on the next attempt.
skills.guidance: Offered by staff after sustained observed readiness. The role involves agreed volunteer shifts and training successors.
skills.unlocks: A named apron, dedicated storage nook, and agreed volunteer shifts with recorded hours.
